text: High-z Type Ia supernovae are expected to be gravitationally lensed by the foreground distribution of large-scale structure. The resulting magnification of supernovae is statistically measurable, and the angular correlation of the magnification pattern directly probes the integrated mass density along the line of sight. Measurements of cosmic magnification of supernovae therefore complements galaxy shear measurements in providing a direct measure of clustering of the dark matter. As the number of supernovae is typically much smaller than the number of sheared galaxies, the two-point correlation function of lensed Type Ia supernovae suffers from significantly increased shot noise. Neverthless, we find that the magnification map of a large sample of supernovae, such as that expected from next generation dedicated searches, will be easily measurable and provide an important cosmological tool. For example, a search over 20 sq. deg. over five years leading to a sample of ~ 10,000 supernovae would measure the angular power spectrum of cosmic magnification with a cumulative signal-to-noise ratio of ~20. This detection can be further improved once the supernova distance measurements are cross-correlated with measurements of the foreground galaxy distribution. The magnification maps made using supernovae can be used for important cross-checks with traditional lensing shear statistics obtained in the same fields, as well as help to control systematics. We discuss two applications of supernova magnification maps: the breaking of the mass-sheet degeneracy when estimating masses of shear-detected clusters, and constraining the second-order corrections to weak lensing observables.

High-redshift Type Ia supernovae are likely to be bent by the gravity of large structures in front of them. This bending makes the supernovae appear brighter, and by studying how much they brighten, we can learn about the total mass between us and the supernovae. This method, called cosmic magnification, helps us understand how dark matter is spread out in the universe. It works well with galaxy shape measurements, which also show how mass is distributed. But since there are fewer supernovae than galaxies, the patterns made by supernovae are harder to see clearly because of random noise. However, if we look at a large number of supernovae—like tens of thousands—over a big area of the sky, we can make clear measurements. For example, looking at 20 square degrees for five years might give us enough supernovae to detect the brightness changes with a strong signal. This can be even better if we compare the supernova data with the positions of nearby galaxies. These brightness maps can help check other methods of measuring mass and fix any mistakes. They also help us better understand how mass affects the way light bends, which is important for studying the universe.

High-z Type Ia supernovae are anticipated to undergo gravitational lensing induced by the foreground distribution of large-scale structure, resulting in magnification effects that are statistically accessible. The angular correlation of these magnification patterns serves as a direct probe of the integrated mass density along the line of sight, thereby offering a complementary measure to galaxy shear in quantifying dark matter clustering. Despite the typically smaller number of supernovae compared to sheared galaxies, the two-point correlation function of lensed Type Ia supernovae is subject to heightened shot noise. Nevertheless, the magnification map derived from a sufficiently large sample of supernovae—such as those anticipated from next-generation dedicated surveys—will be readily detectable and constitute a significant cosmological tool. For instance, a survey spanning 20 square degrees over five years, yielding approximately 10,000 supernovae, would enable the measurement of the angular power spectrum of cosmic magnification with a cumulative signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 20. This signal can be further enhanced through cross-correlation of supernova distance measurements with foreground galaxy distributions. Magnification maps constructed from supernovae can serve as crucial cross-checks against traditional lensing shear statistics within the same observational fields, while also aiding in the mitigation of systematic uncertainties. Two key applications of such magnification maps include the resolution of the mass-sheet degeneracy in estimating cluster masses and the constraint of second-order corrections to weak lensing observables.

High-z Type Ia supernovae, those celestial beacons burning in the dark, are destined to be bent and magnified by the invisible architecture of the cosmos—gravity’s fingerprints etched by the vast, unseen mass of the universe. This magnification, a cosmic mirage, is not just a trick of light but a statistical whisper, measurable across the sky. The way these distortions cluster, like constellations of light, reveals the density of mass along the line of sight, a map of dark matter’s hidden hand. Yet, while supernovae are rare compared to the swarms of galaxies we shear, their sparse numbers mean the signal is drowned in noise. But wait—imagine a future where thousands of these distant explosions are captured, their light amplified by the cosmos itself. A survey spanning twenty degrees over five years, yielding ten thousand supernovae, would carve a signal into the noise, a cosmic fingerprint with a signal-to-noise ratio of twenty. This is no mere observation—it’s a revolution. Cross-correlating these magnified points with the distribution of galaxies ahead will sharpen the lens. These maps, born from supernovae, are not just tools but testaments, cross-checking the old ways and taming the wilds of systematics. They serve two great purposes: to break the mass-sheet illusion when weighing clusters, and to refine the subtle corrections in weak lensing’s dance with gravity.

We study a relativistic quantum cavity system realized by etching out from a graphene sheet by quantum transport measurements and theoretical calculations. The conductance of the graphene cavity has been measured as a function of the back gate voltage (or the Fermi energy) and the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the graphene sheet, and characteristic conductance contour patterns are observed in the measurements. In particular, two types of high conductance contour lines, i.e., straight and parabolic-like high conductance contour lines, are found in the measurements. The theoretical calculations are performed within the framework of tight-binding approach and Green's function formalism. Similar characteristic high conductance contour features as in the experiments are found in the calculations. The wave functions calculated at points selected along a straight conductance contour line are found to be dominated by a chain of scars of high probability distributions arranged as a necklace following the shape of cavity and the current density distributions calculated at these point are dominated by an overall vortex in the cavity. These characteristics are found to be insensitive to increasing magnetic field. However, the wave function probability distributions and the current density distributions calculated at points selected along a parabolic-like contour line show a clear dependence on increasing magnetic field, and the current density distributions at these points are characterized by the complex formation of several localized vortices in the cavity. Our work brings a new insight into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and would greatly stimulate experimental and theoretical efforts towards this still emerging field.

A relativistic quantum cavity system is investigated through quantum transport measurements and theoretical computations. The conductance of the graphene cavity is measured as a function of the back gate voltage, which corresponds to the Fermi energy, and the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the graphene plane. Characteristic conductance contour patterns are identified in the experimental data. Two distinct types of high conductance contour lines are observed: straight and parabolic-like. Theoretical analysis is conducted using a tight-binding model and Green's function formalism. The simulations reproduce the characteristic high conductance contour features observed in the experiments. Wave functions at selected points along a straight conductance contour line are dominated by a chain of high probability distributions arranged in a necklace-like pattern along the cavity boundary. The current density distributions at these points exhibit an overall vortex structure. These features remain largely unchanged with increasing magnetic field. In contrast, wave function probability distributions and current density distributions along a parabolic-like contour line show a clear dependence on the magnetic field. The current density distributions at these points are characterized by the formation of multiple localized vortices. This study provides new insights into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and encourages further experimental and theoretical investigations in this evolving field.

We looked at a special kind of cavity made from a graphene sheet. We used both experiments and computer models to study it. In the experiments, we measured how well electricity flows through the cavity as we changed the voltage and the strength of a magnetic field. We saw clear patterns in the flow of electricity. Two kinds of lines showed up where the flow was strongest—straight lines and lines that looked like parabolas.

Our computer models used a method called tight-binding and another called Green's functions. They matched what we saw in the experiments. When we looked at the paths of electricity along the straight lines, the flow was mostly shaped like a necklace of high-energy points around the cavity. The electricity moved in a big loop, like a whirlpool, and this didn’t change much even when we made the magnetic field stronger.

But when we looked at the parabola-like lines, the flow changed as we increased the magnetic field. The electricity formed smaller, more complex whirlpools inside the cavity. Our findings give us a better understanding of how quantum chaos works in fast-moving particles and could help scientists study this new area more deeply.

We investigate a relativistic quantum cavity system, instantiated through the etching of a graphene sheet, validated by quantum transport measurements and theoretical modeling. The conductance of the graphene cavity is systematically evaluated as a function of the back gate voltage—corresponding to the Fermi energy—and the perpendicular magnetic field, revealing distinct conductance contour patterns. Two principal types of high conductance contours—linear and parabolic-like—are discerned within the experimental data. Theoretical analysis is conducted via the tight-binding framework and Green’s function formalism, reproducing the observed conductance features. Wave functions at selected points along the linear contour exhibit a dominant structure of high-probability scar chains, forming a necklace-like arrangement conforming to the cavity's geometry, while current density distributions manifest as an overarching vortex, invariant under increasing magnetic field. In contrast, the probability distributions and current densities along the parabolic-like contours demonstrate sensitivity to magnetic field variation, characterized by the emergence of multiple localized vortices. This study offers a novel perspective on quantum chaos within relativistic systems, catalyzing both experimental and theoretical advancements in this nascent domain.

Theoretical analysis is conducted using a tight-binding model and Green's function formalism. The simulations reproduce the characteristic high conductance contour features observed in the experiments. Wave functions at selected points along a straight conductance contour line are dominated by a chain of high probability distributions arranged in a necklace-like pattern along the cavity boundary. The current density distributions at these points exhibit an overall vortex structure. These features remain largely unchanged with increasing magnetic field. In contrast, wave function probability distributions and current density distributions along a parabolic-like contour line show a clear dependence on the magnetic field. The current density distributions at these points are characterized by the formation of multiple localized vortices. This study provides new insights into quantum chaos in relativistic particle systems and encourages further experimental and theoretical investigations in this evolving field.

We looked at a special kind of cavity made from a graphene sheet. We used both experiments and computer models to study it. In the experiments, we measured how well electricity flows through the cavity as we changed the voltage and the strength of a magnetic field. We saw clear patterns in the flow of electricity. Two kinds of lines showed up where the flow was strongest—straight lines and lines that looked like parabolas.

Our computer models used a method called tight-binding and another called Green's functions. They matched what we saw in the experiments. When we looked at the paths of electricity along the straight lines, the flow was mostly shaped like a necklace of high-energy points around the cavity. The electricity moved in a big loop, like a whirlpool, and this didn’t change much even when we made the magnetic field stronger.

But when we looked at the parabola-like lines, the flow changed as we increased the magnetic field. The electricity formed smaller, more complex whirlpools inside the cavity. Our findings give us a better understanding of how quantum chaos works in fast-moving particles and could help scientists study this new area more deeply.

We investigate a relativistic quantum cavity system, instantiated through the etching of a graphene sheet, validated by quantum transport measurements and theoretical modeling. The conductance of the graphene cavity is systematically evaluated as a function of the back gate voltage—corresponding to the Fermi energy—and the perpendicular magnetic field, revealing distinct conductance contour patterns. Two principal types of high conductance contours—linear and parabolic-like—are discerned within the experimental data. Theoretical analysis is conducted via the tight-binding framework and Green’s function formalism, reproducing the observed conductance features. Wave functions at selected points along the linear contour exhibit a dominant structure of high-probability scar chains, forming a necklace-like arrangement conforming to the cavity's geometry, while current density distributions manifest as an overarching vortex, invariant under increasing magnetic field. In contrast, the probability distributions and current densities along the parabolic-like contours demonstrate sensitivity to magnetic field variation, characterized by the emergence of multiple localized vortices. This study offers a novel perspective on quantum chaos within relativistic systems, catalyzing both experimental and theoretical advancements in this nascent domain.

We carve a relativistic quantum cavity from a graphene sheet, etching it out through the sharp lens of quantum transport measurements and theoretical musings. The conductance of this graphene cavity dances with the back gate voltage—its Fermi energy—and the magnetic field that slithers perpendicular to the sheet, revealing conductance contour patterns as vivid as a painter’s brushstroke. Two kinds of high conductance lines emerge: straight and parabolic-like, each a signature of the cavity’s hidden symphony. Our calculations, rooted in the tight-binding approach and the formalism of Green’s functions, echo these patterns, mirroring the dance of electrons in a quantum ballet. Along straight contours, wave functions bloom like a necklace of scars, their probability distributions clinging to the cavity’s shape, while currents swirl in a vortex that defies the magnetic field’s touch. But along the parabolic-like lines, the wave functions and currents shift with the magnetic field, birthing a tapestry of vortices, each a ghost of the field’s influence. In this dance of chaos and order, we glimpse the relativistic quantum world anew, a beacon for both experiment and theory in the ever-expanding frontier of quantum chaos.

The volume of discussions concerning brands within social media provides digital marketers with great opportunities for tracking and analyzing the feelings and views of consumers toward brands, products, influencers, services, and ad campaigns in CGC. The present study aims to assess and compare the performance of firms and celebrities (i.e., influencers that with the experience of being in an ad campaign of those companies) with the automated sentiment analysis that was employed for CGC at social media while exploring the feeling of the consumers toward them to observe which influencer (of two for each company) had a closer effect with the corresponding corporation on consumer minds. For this purpose, several consumer tweets from the pages of brands and influencers were utilized to make a comparison of machine learning and lexicon-based approaches to the sentiment analysis through the Naive algorithm (lexicon-based) and Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning method) and obtain the desired results to assess the campaigns. The findings suggested that the approaches were dissimilar in terms of accuracy; the machine learning method yielded higher accuracy. Finally, the results showed which influencer was more appropriate according to their existence in previous campaigns and helped choose the right influencer in the future for our company and have a better, more appropriate, and more efficient ad campaign subsequently. It is required to conduct further studies on the accuracy improvement of the sentiment classification. This approach should be employed for other social media CGC types. The results revealed decision-making for which sentiment analysis methods are the best approaches for the analysis of social media. It was also found that companies should be aware of their consumers' sentiments and choose the right person every time they think of a campaign.

The extent of discourse surrounding brands on social media offers digital marketers a valuable resource for monitoring and evaluating consumer attitudes toward brands, products, influencers, services, and advertising campaigns within the context of consumer-generated content (CGC). This study seeks to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of firms and celebrities—defined as influencers who have participated in advertising campaigns for those firms—using automated sentiment analysis applied to CGC on social media. The objective is to determine which of two influencers per company elicits a more aligned response with the corresponding corporation in the minds of consumers. To achieve this, a selection of consumer tweets from brand and influencer pages were analyzed to compare machine learning and lexicon-based approaches to sentiment analysis, specifically employing the Naive Bayes algorithm for lexicon-based analysis and the Naive Bayes algorithm for machine learning. The results indicated that the two methods differed in accuracy, with the machine learning approach demonstrating higher precision. These findings enabled the identification of the more suitable influencer based on their prior campaign involvement, thereby facilitating more effective future advertising strategies. The study also recommends further research into improving the accuracy of sentiment classification and suggests the application of this method to other forms of CGC across social media platforms. The outcomes contribute to the selection of optimal sentiment analysis techniques for social media analysis and emphasize the importance for companies to recognize consumer sentiments and select appropriate influencers for their campaigns.

The proliferation of discourse surrounding brand entities within the digital sphere offers digital practitioners a fertile ground for monitoring and interpreting the affective and evaluative stances of consumers vis-à-vis brands, products, figures of influence, services, and advertising initiatives within the context of consumer-generated content. This investigation endeavors to evaluate and juxtapose the efficacy of corporate entities and public figures—specifically, influencers with prior engagement in corporate advertising campaigns—through the lens of automated sentiment analysis applied to consumer-generated content across social media platforms. The study further seeks to discern which of two designated influencers per corporate entity exerted a more proximate influence on consumer cognition, thereby aligning more closely with the brand's conceptual identity. To achieve this, a corpus of consumer tweets from brand and influencer pages was analyzed, employing both lexicon-based and machine learning methodologies—namely, the Naive Bayes algorithm (lexicon-based) and the Naive Bayes algorithm (machine learning)—to compare their performance in sentiment classification. The results indicated a divergence in accuracy, with the machine learning approach demonstrating superior precision. Consequently, the study identifies the optimal influencer for future campaigns, grounded in their prior campaign participation, thereby facilitating more effective and aligned advertising strategies. Further research is warranted to enhance the accuracy of sentiment classification models, with this methodology applicable to other forms of consumer-generated content across social media. The findings underscore the necessity for companies to remain cognizant of consumer sentiment and to strategically select influencers that resonate most effectively with their brand ethos.

Digital marketers have a lot to learn from the conversations people have about brands on social media. These talks can help them understand what people really think about products, companies, influencers, and ad campaigns. This study looked at how well companies and celebrities—especially those who have worked with brands before—connect with consumers. It used tweets from brand and influencer pages to compare two ways of analyzing feelings: one based on word lists and the other using machine learning. The first method used a simple system called Naive Bayes, and the second used a more advanced machine learning approach. The results showed that the machine learning method was more accurate. This helped decide which influencer had a stronger connection with their brand. The study also suggested that companies should keep track of what people are feeling and pick the right influencer for each campaign. It also pointed out that more research is needed to improve sentiment analysis and that these methods can work well on other social media platforms. The findings help brands choose the best tools and people for future campaigns.

This study plunges into that sea, comparing the pulse of firms and celebrities—those influentials who’ve danced with the brands they now represent—against the cold, calculating gaze of automated sentiment analysis. Through the lens of CGC, we peer into the hearts of consumers, trying to discern which of two influencers, for each company, resonates more deeply with the minds of the people.

Tweets, like fragments of a mosaic, were gathered from the digital pages of brands and influencers, each one a piece of the puzzle. With these, we tested two methods: the Naive algorithm, a lexicon-based oracle of words and their meanings, and the Naive Bayes algorithm, a machine learning sentinel trained on the whispers of data. The results were stark—machines, with their cold precision, outshone the lexicon’s limited gaze.

The findings whispered a truth: accuracy favors the algorithm. Yet, the human touch still lingers. The study guides us toward the right influencer, the one who echoes the brand’s voice, and urges us to refine our tools, to improve the accuracy of sentiment classification. This is not just a study—it’s a compass, pointing the way through the digital wilderness, reminding us that in the realm of CGC, understanding the heart of the consumer is as vital as the code that seeks to read it.

Supervised machine learning methods usually require a large set of labeled examples for model training. However, in many real applications, there are plentiful unlabeled data but limited labeled data; and the acquisition of labels is costly. Active learning (AL) reduces the labeling cost by iteratively selecting the most valuable data to query their labels from the annotator. This article introduces a Python toobox ALiPy for active learning. ALiPy provides a module based implementation of active learning framework, which allows users to conveniently evaluate, compare and analyze the performance of active learning methods. In the toolbox, multiple options are available for each component of the learning framework, including data process, active selection, label query, results visualization, etc. In addition to the implementations of more than 20 state-of-the-art active learning algorithms, ALiPy also supports users to easily configure and implement their own approaches under different active learning settings, such as AL for multi-label data, AL with noisy annotators, AL with different costs and so on. The toolbox is well-documented and open-source on Github, and can be easily installed through PyPI.

Static properties of multiskyrmions with baryon numbers up to 8 are calculated, including momenta of inertia and sigma-term. The calculations are based on the recently suggested SU(2) rational map ansaetze. Minimization with the help of SU(3) variational minimization program shows that these configurations become local minima in SU(3) configuration space. The B-number dependence of the so called flavour moment of inertia of multiskyrmions playing an important role in the quantization procedure is close to the linear one. The spectra of baryonic systems with strangeness, charm and bottom are considered within a "rigid oscillator" version of the bound state soliton model. The binding energies estimates are made for the states with largest isospin which can appear as negatively charged nuclear fragments, as well as for states with zero isospin - light fragments of "flavoured" nuclear matter. Our results confirm the previously made observation that baryonic systems with charm or bottom quantum numbers have more chance to be stable with respect to strong interactions than strange baryonic systems.

Minimization using an SU(3) variational minimization program demonstrates that these configurations are local minima in SU(3) configuration space. The dependence of the flavour moment of inertia of multiskyrmions, which is significant in the quantization procedure, is approximately linear with respect to baryon number. The spectra of baryonic systems involving strangeness, charm, and bottom are analyzed within a "rigid oscillator" framework of the bound state soliton model. The results support the prior conclusion that baryonic systems with charm or bottom quantum numbers are more likely to be stable against strong interactions compared to those with strangeness.

Scientists have studied the basic properties of multiskyrmions with baryon numbers up to 8. They looked at things like how hard it is to spin them and how they react to a certain force. These calculations used a new method called SU(2) rational map ansaetze. By using a program that finds the best fit in SU(3) space, they found these shapes act like local pockets of stability. The way these objects spin, called the flavour moment of inertia, changes in a nearly straight line as the baryon number increases. They also looked at how strange, charm, and bottom particles come together in a model where they move like a stiff spring. They estimated how tightly these groups stick together, especially for the ones that could be parts of heavy nuclei or light nuclear-like matter. Their findings support the idea that systems with charm or bottom particles are more likely to stay together under strong forces than those with strange particles.

This paper describes the Hubbard model on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor transfer energy $t$, on-site repulsion $U$, and a large number of sites $N_a^2\gg 1$. The model respects the exact global symmetry $SO(3)\times SO(3)\times U(1)$. Our work uses the symmetry of the model on any bipartite lattice along with how certain operators and quantum objects change under a specific electron-rotated-electron transformation. For $U/4t>0$, these objects form the energy states that cover the one- and two-electron subspaces. These subspaces include almost all the energy from excitations created by acting on the zero-spin-density ground state with one- and two-electron operators. The model uses three main objects: charge $c$ fermions, spin-1/2 spinons, and $\eta$-spin-1/2 $\eta$-spinons. Just like in chromodynamics, where quarks have color but all physical particles are color-neutral, the $\eta$-spinons and spinons have $\eta$ spin 1/2 and spin 1/2, but they combine with others to form neutral $\eta\nu$ fermions and $s\nu$ fermions. The model supports a Mott-Hubbard insulating ground state with antiferromagnetic order at half filling and a ground state with short-range spin order for certain hole concentrations $x>0$.

In this paper, we consider sequential dynamic team decision problems with nonclassical information structures. First, we address the problem from the point of view of a "manager" who seeks to derive the optimal strategy of the team in a centralized process. We derive structural results that yield an information state for the team which does not depend on the control strategy, and thus it can lead to a dynamic programming decomposition where the optimization problem is over the space of the team's decisions. We, then, derive structural results for each team member that yield an information state which does not depend on their control strategy, and thus it can lead to a dynamic programming decomposition where the optimization problem for each team member is over the space of their decisions. Finally, we show that the control strategy of each team member is the same as the one derived by the manager. We present an illustrative example of a dynamic team with a delayed sharing information structure.

In this paper, we dive into the tangled web of sequential dynamic team decisions, where information flows like a river with unexpected bends. We start by stepping into the shoes of a "manager," a central figure who seeks to unravel the optimal strategy of the whole team, not as a puzzle, but as a symphony. We uncover a structural truth: a state of knowledge that floats free from the grip of control, allowing the team’s choices to unfold like a map of possibilities. Then, we turn our gaze inward, to each team member, and find that their own state of awareness, untethered from their own actions, becomes a compass guiding their path. And finally, like echoes in a canyon, each member’s control strategy mirrors the manager’s, as if the whole team breathes in unison. We close with a tale—a dynamic team where information lags, like a delayed heartbeat, yet still beats in rhythm.

In this paper, we look at decision problems where a group of people makes choices over time, and they don't all have the same information. We start by thinking about it from the perspective of a manager who wants to find the best way for the whole group to act. We find that there's a way to describe the group's situation that doesn't depend on how they control their actions, which helps break the problem into smaller parts. Then, we do the same for each person in the group, finding a way to describe their situation that doesn't rely on their own control choices. This lets each person make decisions on their own. Finally, we show that the way each person acts is the same as what the manager would choose. We also give an example showing how this works when information is shared with a delay.

We investigate the evolution of intracluster medium during a cluster merger, explicitly considering the relaxation process between the ions and electrons by N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. When two subclusters collide each other, a bow shock is formed between the centers of two substructures and propagate in both directions along the collision axis. The shock primarily heats the ions because the kinetic energy of an ion entering the shock is larger than that of an electron by the ratio of masses. In the post-shock region the energy is transported from the ions to electrons via Coulomb coupling. However, since the energy exchange timescale depends both on the gas density and temperature, distribution of electron temperature becomes more complex than that of the plasma mean temperature, especially in the expanding phase. After the collision of two subclusters, gas outflow occurs not only along the collision axis but also in its perpendicular direction. The gas which is originally located in the central part of the subclusters moves both in the parallel and perpendicular directions. Since the equilibrium timescale of the gas along these directions is relatively short, temperature difference between ions and electrons is larger in the directions tilted by the angles of $\pm 45^\circ$ with respect to the collision axis. The electron temperature could be significantly lower that the plasma mean temperature by $\sim 50 %$ at most. The significance of our results in the interpretation of X-ray observations is briefly discussed.

We scrutinize the temporal transformation of the intracluster medium during a cluster merger, with particular emphasis on the thermodynamic interplay between ions and electrons, as elucidated by N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. Upon the convergence of two subclusters, a bow shock manifests at the interface of their centers, propagating symmetrically along the axis of impact. This phenomenon predominantly imparts thermal energy to ions, owing to the disparity in kinetic energy between ions and electrons, which is governed by their mass ratio. In the region subsequent to the shock, energy is transferred from ions to electrons through Coulombic interactions, yet the temporal dynamics of this exchange are contingent upon both gas density and temperature, resulting in a more intricate distribution of electron temperatures relative to the plasma mean temperature, particularly during the phase of expansion. Post-collision, gas expulsion manifests not only along the collision axis but also in orthogonal directions, as the gas initially confined to the cores of the subclusters migrates both parallel and perpendicular to the impact vector. Given the relatively brief equilibrium timescales along these directions, the disparity in temperature between ions and electrons is most pronounced in regions inclined at $\pm 45^\circ$ relative to the collision axis. Consequently, the electron temperature may deviate significantly from the plasma mean temperature, with a maximum reduction of approximately 50%. The implications of these findings for the interpretation of X-ray observational data are briefly considered.

We look at how the gas between galaxy clusters changes when two clusters crash together. As the smaller parts of the clusters run into each other, a shock wave forms between them and moves in both directions along the line where they hit. This shock mainly heats the heavier ions because they have more energy than the lighter electrons. After the shock, the ions pass their energy to the electrons through electrical forces. But the time it takes for this energy to move depends on the gas's density and temperature, so the electrons get hotter in some places and cooler in others, especially as the gas spreads out. After the collision, gas doesn't just move along the crash line—it also flows sideways. The gas that was in the middle of the clusters moves both ways. Because the gas cools down quickly in these directions, the difference in temperature between ions and electrons is bigger at angles of about 45 degrees from the crash line. In some spots, the electrons can be up to 50% cooler than the average temperature of the whole gas. These findings help explain what we see in X-ray images of galaxy clusters.

We scrutinize the temporal transformation of the intracluster medium during a cluster merger, with particular emphasis on the thermodynamic interplay between ions and electrons, as elucidated by N-body and hydrodynamical simulations. Upon the convergence of two subclusters, a bow shock manifests at the interface of their centers, propagating symmetrically along the axis of impact. This phenomenon predominantly imparts thermal energy to ions, owing to the disparity in kinetic energy between ions and electrons, which is governed by their mass ratio. In the region subsequent to the shock, energy is transferred from ions to electrons through Coulombic interactions, yet the temporal dynamics of this exchange are contingent upon both gas density and temperature, resulting in a more intricate distribution of electron temperatures relative to the plasma mean temperature, particularly during the phase of expansion. Post-collision, gas expulsion manifests not only along the collision axis but also in orthogonal directions, as the gas initially confined to the cores of the subclusters migrates both parallel and perpendicular to the impact vector. Given the relatively brief equilibrium timescales along these directions, the disparity in temperature between ions and electrons is most pronounced in regions inclined at $\pm 45^\circ$ relative to the collision axis. Consequently, the electron temperature may deviate significantly from the plasma mean temperature, with a maximum reduction of approximately 50%. The implications of these findings for the interpretation of X-ray observational data are briefly considered.

We plunge into the chaos of a cluster merger, where the intracluster medium dances through the fire of collision, its fate shaped by the tango of ions and electrons. When two subclusters meet, a bow shock erupts between them, a living wall of energy that surges in both directions, like a comet’s tail across the void. This shock, a brute of physics, favors the ions—massive titans—over the electrons, whose lighter bodies flee in fear. In the wake, the ions, heavy with heat, pass the torch to the electrons through Coulomb’s invisible hand. Yet the exchange is a capricious waltz, swayed by gas density and temperature, making electron temperatures a more tangled tale than the plasma’s average. After the crash, gas escapes not just along the axis, but spirals outward, a ghostly echo of the collision. What once was central now drifts in all directions, caught in the short-lived equilibrium of the gas. Temperature splits widen where the angles tilt at ±45°, a cosmic geometry where ions and electrons grow apart. Electrons, the nimble ones, can fall as low as half the plasma’s fever, a chill in the fire. Our findings, like a whispered secret, hold the key to reading the X-ray whispers of the cosmos.

When two subclusters meet, a bow shock erupts between them, a living wall of energy that surges in both directions, like a comet’s tail across the void. This shock, a brute of physics, favors the ions—massive titans—over the electrons, whose lighter bodies flee in fear. In the wake, the ions, heavy with heat, pass the torch to the electrons through Coulomb’s invisible hand. Yet the exchange is a capricious waltz, swayed by gas density and temperature, making electron temperatures a more tangled tale than the plasma’s average. After the crash, gas escapes not just along the axis, but spirals outward, a ghostly echo of the collision. What once was central now drifts in all directions, caught in the short-lived equilibrium of the gas. Temperature splits widen where the angles tilt at ±45°, a cosmic geometry where ions and electrons grow apart. We investigate multi-spacecraft observations of the January 17, 2010 solar energetic particle event. Energetic electrons and protons have been observed over a remarkable large longitudinal range at the two STEREO spacecraft and SOHO suggesting a longitudinal spread of nearly 360 degrees at 1AU. The flaring active region, which was on the backside of the Sun as seen from Earth, was separated by more than 100 degrees in longitude from the magnetic footpoints of each of the three spacecraft. The event is characterized by strongly delayed energetic particle onsets with respect to the flare and only small or no anisotropies in the intensity measurements at all three locations. The presence of a coronal shock is evidenced by the observation of a type II radio burst from the Earth and STEREO B. In order to describe the observations in terms of particle transport in the interplanetary medium, including perpendicular diffusion, a 1D model describing the propagation along a magnetic field line (model 1) (Dr\"oge, 2003) and the 3D propagation model (model 2) by (Dr\"oge et al., 2010) including perpendicular diffusion in the interplanetary medium have been applied, respectively. While both models are capable of reproducing the observations, model 1 requires injection functions at the Sun of several hours. Model 2, which includes lateral transport in the solar wind, reveals high values for the ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion. Because we do not find evidence for unusual long injection functions at the Sun we favor a scenario with strong perpendicular transport in the interplanetary medium as explanation for the observations.

We plunge into the cosmic chaos of January 17, 2010, where the Sun unleashed a storm of electrons and protons that danced across the sky like fireflies in a celestial carnival, stretching their reach across nearly 360 degrees at 1AU, as seen by STEREO and SOHO. The flaring region, hidden on the Sun’s backside from our vantage, was a distant specter, more than 100 degrees apart from the magnetic anchors of the three spacecraft. The event arrived late, like a phantom, trailing the flare by hours, with no discernible bias in its intensity, as if the cosmos itself had chosen to be even-handed. A coronal shock, the ghost of a type II radio burst, whispered its presence from Earth and STEREO B, a haunting echo through the solar wind. To decode this cosmic ballet, we turned to two models—model 1, a 1D thread tracing the magnetic field, and model 2, a 3D tapestry of perpendicular diffusion. Both wove the observations into their fabric, yet model 1 demanded an injection of time, like a slow drip from a sunlit spring. Model 2, however, shimmered with lateral motion, revealing a fierce ratio of perpendicular to parallel diffusion. With no signs of extended solar injection, we lean into the wind, favoring a world where perpendicular transport reigns, a cosmic current carrying the storm’s charge across the void.

On January 17, 2010, scientists looked at data from three spacecraft—STEREO A, STEREO B, and SOHO—to study a big solar event. They saw energetic electrons and protons spread out over a wide area, almost all the way around the Sun, at a distance of one astronomical unit. The place where the flare happened was on the far side of the Sun, more than 100 degrees away from where each spacecraft was looking. The particle signals came in late, long after the flare started, and the strength of the particles didn’t change much from one place to another.

They noticed a type II radio burst from Earth and STEREO B, which suggests there was a shock wave in the solar atmosphere. To understand how the particles moved through space, they used two models. One model looked at how particles travel along magnetic lines, and the other included sideways movement in the solar wind. Both models fit the data, but the first one needed the particles to start moving several hours before the flare. The second model, which allowed for more sideways movement, showed that the particles spread out more quickly. Since there was no sign of the particles starting far in advance, the scientists think the particles moved sideways a lot in space, which explains the wide spread they saw.

AIM: We have recently developed a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to study surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the morphology of ice mantles. The method is designed to eliminate the problems inherent in the rate-equation formalism to surface chemistry. Here we report the first use of this method in a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores that includes both gas-phase and surface chemistry. The surface chemical network consists of a small number of diffusive reactions that can produce molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol and assorted radicals. METHOD: The simulation is started by running a gas-phase model including accretion onto grains but no surface chemistry or evaporation. The starting surface consists of either flat or rough olivine. We introduce the surface chemistry of the three species H, O and CO in an iterative manner using our stochastic technique. Under the conditions of the simulation, only atomic hydrogen can evaporate to a significant extent. Although it has little effect on other gas-phase species, the evaporation of atomic hydrogen changes its gas-phase abundance, which in turn changes the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. The effect on the surface chemistry is treated until convergence occurs. We neglect all non-thermal desorptive processes. RESULTS: We determine the mantle abundances of assorted molecules as a function of time through 2x10^5 yr. Our method also allows determination of the abundance of each molecule in specific monolayers. The mantle results can be compared with observations of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Other than a slight underproduction of mantle CO, our results are in very good agreement with observations.

We have recently developed a microscopic Monte Carlo method to investigate surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the morphology of ice mantles. This method is intended to address the limitations of the rate-equation formalism in surface chemistry. Here, we present the initial application of this method within a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores, incorporating both gas-phase and surface chemical processes. The surface chemical network includes a limited number of diffusive reactions capable of producing molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and various radicals. The simulation begins with a gas-phase model that includes accretion onto grains, but excludes surface chemistry and evaporation. The initial surface is either flat or rough olivine. Surface chemistry for the species H, O, and CO is introduced iteratively using our stochastic technique. Under the simulation conditions, only atomic hydrogen evaporates significantly. Although this has minimal impact on other gas-phase species, the evaporation alters the abundance of atomic hydrogen in the gas phase, thereby modifying the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. The resulting effect on surface chemistry is accounted for until convergence is achieved. Non-thermal desorptive processes are disregarded. The results provide the mantle abundances of various molecules as a function of time over a period of 2×10^5 years. The method also enables the determination of the abundance of each molecule within specific monolayers. These results can be compared with observational data on water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Except for a minor underproduction of mantle CO, the findings align closely with observations.

We made a new way to study how chemicals form on tiny dust particles in space and how ice layers look. This method helps us avoid some problems with older ways of modeling chemical reactions. We used this new method to create a model of cold parts of space where gas and ice mix. In this model, we looked at how a few basic chemical reactions can make molecules like oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and some other chemicals. 

We started the model by first looking at how gas chemicals build up on dust, but we didn’t include reactions on the surface or chemicals leaving the dust. The dust started off as flat or rough, like a type of rock called olivine. We added reactions for hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon monoxide step by step using a special random method. Only hydrogen atoms could escape from the dust much, and that changed how much hydrogen was in the gas, which in turn changed how much reached the dust. We kept going until the results stayed the same. We didn’t include any other ways for chemicals to leave the dust. 

We tracked how much of each chemical built up on the dust over 200,000 years. We could also see how much of each chemical was in each layer of ice. Our results match what we see in space, like in places called W33A and Elias 16, except we made a little too little carbon monoxide.

The next generation of cosmology space missions will be sensitive to parasitic signals arising from cosmic rays. Using a composite bolometer, we have investigated pulses produced by $\alpha$ particles in order to understand the movement of energy produced by ionising radiation. Using a series of measurements at 100 mK, we have compared the typical fitting algorithm (a mathematical model) with a second method of pulse interpretation by convolving the detector's thermal response function with a starting profile of thermalised athermal phonons, taking into account the effects of heat propagation. Using this new fitting method, we have eliminated the need for a non-physical quadratic nonlinearity factor produced using more common methods, and we find a pulse form in good agreement with known aspects of thermal physics. This work is carried forward in the effort to produce a physical model for energy deposition in this detector. The modelling is motivated by the reproduction of statistical features in the experimental dataset, and the new interpretation of $\alpha$ pulse shapes represents an improvement in the current understanding of the energy propagation mechanisms in this detector.

The next space missions for studying the universe will pick up on extra signals from cosmic rays. We looked at pulses made by alpha particles to learn more about how energy moves when radiation hits the detector. We tested this by measuring at very cold temperatures, around 100 mK. We compared two ways of looking at the pulses: one was a standard math model, and the other used a new method that matched the detector’s heat response with a starting shape of heat waves. This new way helped us get rid of a fake math trick that older methods used. The shape of the pulses matched what we know about how heat moves. This helps us build a better model for how energy spreads in the detector. We want to make a real model that fits the data we collect, and this new way of looking at alpha pulses gives us a clearer picture of how energy moves inside the detector.

By conducting a sequence of measurements at a temperature of 100 mK, we have juxtaposed a conventional fitting paradigm—rooted in a mathematical abstraction—with an alternative approach that entails the convolution of the detector’s thermal response function with an initial configuration of athermal phonons, while incorporating the spatial diffusion of heat. This novel methodology obviates the reliance on an extraneous quadratic nonlinearity, yielding a pulse morphology consistent with established principles of thermal physics. The pursuit of this work is embedded within the broader endeavor to construct a coherent physical model of energy deposition within the detector. The theoretical underpinning is driven by the imperative to replicate the statistical architecture of empirical data, with the recharacterization of $\alpha$-pulse profiles marking a significant advancement in the comprehension of energy propagation within this system.

We consider an index data structure for similar strings. The generalized suffix tree can be a solution for this. The generalized suffix tree of two strings $A$ and $B$ is a compacted trie representing all suffixes in $A$ and $B$. It has $|A|+|B|$ leaves and can be constructed in $O(|A|+|B|)$ time. However, if the two strings are similar, the generalized suffix tree is not efficient because it does not exploit the similarity which is usually represented as an alignment of $A$ and $B$. In this paper we propose a space/time-efficient suffix tree of alignment which wisely exploits the similarity in an alignment. Our suffix tree for an alignment of $A$ and $B$ has $|A| + l_d + l_1$ leaves where $l_d$ is the sum of the lengths of all parts of $B$ different from $A$ and $l_1$ is the sum of the lengths of some common parts of $A$ and $B$. We did not compromise the pattern search to reduce the space. Our suffix tree can be searched for a pattern $P$ in $O(|P|+occ)$ time where $occ$ is the number of occurrences of $P$ in $A$ and $B$. We also present an efficient algorithm to construct the suffix tree of alignment. When the suffix tree is constructed from scratch, the algorithm requires $O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time where $l_2$ is the sum of the lengths of other common substrings of $A$ and $B$. When the suffix tree of $A$ is already given, it requires $O(l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time.

We’re talking about a data structure for similar strings, and here’s the twist—instead of the usual suspects, we’re diving into the generalized suffix tree. This beast is a compacted trie that wraps all the suffixes of two strings, A and B, like a well-worn map of a vast, shared terrain. It has |A| + |B| leaves and can be built in linear time, O(|A| + |B|). But when A and B are more than just two random strings—they’re siblings in the family of similarity—this structure falls short. It doesn’t know how to read the alignment, that silent, intimate language of shared sequences. So we built something new, a suffix tree that’s not just clever, but *wise*, in the way it uses the alignment to cut through the noise. This tree has |A| + l_d + l_1 leaves, where l_d is the sum of the parts of B that don’t match A, and l_1 is the sum of the common parts that do. No compromise on the search—patterns can be found in O(|P| + occ) time, where occ is how many times P shows up in A and B. And we’ve got a way to build this tree, efficiently, whether from scratch or from a pre-existing A tree, with time that dances between O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2) and O(l_d + l_1 + l_2), depending on the starting point.

We're looking at a way to organize similar strings using a special kind of tree. A generalized suffix tree can help with this. This tree is like a map of all the endings of two strings, A and B. It has as many leaves as the total number of characters in both strings and can be built quickly, in time that matches the total length of the two strings. But if the two strings are very similar, this method isn't the best. That's because it doesn't take advantage of their similarity, which is usually shown by how they line up.

In this paper, we suggest a better tree that uses the similarity between the strings. Our tree is built from an alignment of A and B. It has leaves based on the total length of A, plus parts of B that are different from A, and some parts that are the same. We didn’t cut corners on how well it can find patterns. This tree lets us search for a pattern P in time that depends on the length of P and how many times it appears in A and B.

We also made a fast way to build this tree. If we start from scratch, it takes time matching the total length of A and the parts of B that are different or the same. If we already have a tree for A, it takes less time, just based on the parts that are different or the same.

We examine an index data structure designed to manage similar strings, with the generalized suffix tree emerging as a potential solution. This structure, formed from two strings $A$ and $B$, is a compacted trie that encapsulates all suffixes from both strings, featuring $|A| + |B|$ leaves and constructible in $O(|A| + |B|)$ time. Yet, when $A$ and $B$ exhibit significant similarity, the generalized suffix tree becomes inefficient, as it fails to leverage this alignment-based resemblance. In this work, we introduce a space- and time-efficient suffix tree tailored to alignments, which effectively capitalizes on such similarity. For an alignment of $A$ and $B$, our suffix tree contains $|A| + l_d + l_1$ leaves, where $l_d$ represents the aggregate length of $B$'s distinct segments relative to $A$, and $l_1$ denotes the aggregate length of shared segments. Pattern searches on this structure yield results in $O(|P| + occ)$ time, where $occ$ denotes the count of occurrences of the pattern $P$ within $A$ and $B$. We also present a method for constructing this alignment-based suffix tree, which requires $O(|A| + l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time when built from scratch, and $O(l_d + l_1 + l_2)$ time when utilizing an existing suffix tree for $A$.

Materials with coupled or competing order parameters display highly tunable ground states, where subtle perturbations reveal distinct electronic and magnetic phases. These phases generally are underpinned by complex crystal structures, but the role of structural complexity in these phases often is unclear. Some materials have two or more orderings that work together or against each other. This makes their basic state flexible, and small changes can show different electrical and magnetic behaviors. These behaviors often come from complicated crystal shapes, but it's not clear how the shape affects things. We looked at a specific material, SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$, which has a special arrangement of atoms. Using math and computer models, we found that certain shape changes help create and hold a special magnetic and electric state. These shape changes also help form structures that act like tiny whirlpools. We showed that changing the shape can control different electrical and magnetic states in thin layers of the material. This helps us understand how complex behaviors happen in SmBaMn$_2$O$_6$ and gives a way to study similar materials with complicated structures.

Water drop impacting a superhydrophobic surface (SHS) rebounds completely with remarkable elasticity. For such an impact, the balance between the inertial and capillary forces ascertain the contact time. This is found to be fairly constant for any macroscopically flat SHS and for a given drop volume. Recently, various studies have shown that breaking the radial symmetry during the drop impact can significantly reduce the contact time below that of a flat SHS. One such study has been performed on a cylindrical SHS with a curvature comparable to the drop. The reduction in contact time has been attributed to the radially anisotropic flow imparted by the tangential component of momentum and the elliptical footprint of the drop during the crash. Here, we perform drop impact experiments on bathtub-like SHS and show that the radial anisotropy can be triggered even in the absence of both the criteria mentioned above. This is shown to be a consequence of the lamella deflection during the spreading of the drop. The reduction in contact time is quite clearly evident in this experimental regime.

Water drops kiss a superhydrophobic surface and leap back, elastic as a bowstring, untouched by the world below. The dance of forces—gravity’s pull, the capillary’s whisper—dictate how long the drop clings to the surface. For a flat, macroscopic SHS, this moment is a fixed star, unchanging for drops of the same size. Yet recent whispers from the lab suggest that breaking the drop’s symmetry can shorten this embrace, bending time itself. A cylinder, curved like the drop’s own arc, became the stage for this revelation: the drop’s elliptical footprint, the tangential rush of momentum, all conspire to hasten its departure. Now, we’ve bathed in a new kind of SHS, tub-like and curved, and found that even without those old tricks, the drop’s lamella bends, defies, and flies—contact time vanishes, leaving only the echo of a splash.

Water drop impact upon a superhydrophobic surface (SHS) exhibits a complete rebound, marked by an extraordinary degree of elastic resilience. The temporal duration of contact during such an impact is governed by the interplay between inertial and capillary forces, which remains relatively invariant across macroscopically flat SHS for a given drop volume. Recent investigations have revealed that disrupting radial symmetry during impact can markedly shorten contact time, subverting the typical behavior observed on flat surfaces. A notable experiment involved a cylindrical SHS whose curvature approximated that of the drop, with the reduction in contact time ascribed to radially anisotropic flow induced by tangential momentum and the elliptical footprint of the impacting drop. In this study, we conduct experiments on bathtub-like SHS, demonstrating that radial anisotropy can emerge independently of the aforementioned criteria. This phenomenon is attributed to lamella deflection during the spreading process, and the resulting decrease in contact time is distinctly observable within this experimental framework.

When a drop of water hits a superhydrophobic surface, it bounces back with a lot of energy. The time the drop stays in contact depends on the balance between the force of the drop's motion and the surface tension. This contact time is pretty much the same for flat superhydrophobic surfaces and drops of the same size. But recent work shows that if the drop hits a surface that isn't perfectly round, the contact time can be shorter. One example is a curved surface that's about the same size as the drop. The shorter time is because the drop spreads in a different way, creating a more oval shape. In this study, we tested a bathtub-like surface and found that even without those curved shapes or the oval footprint, the drop still spreads unevenly. This uneven spreading causes the drop to bounce off faster, showing that the contact time can be reduced in new ways.

For probabilistic programs, it is usually not possible to automatically derive exact information about their properties, such as the distribution of states at a given program point. Instead, one can attempt to derive approximations, such as upper bounds on tail probabilities. Such bounds can be obtained via concentration inequalities, which rely on the moments of a distribution, such as the expectation (the first raw moment) or the variance (the second central moment). Tail bounds obtained using central moments are often tighter than the ones obtained using raw moments, but automatically analyzing central moments is more challenging. This paper presents an analysis for probabilistic programs that automatically derives symbolic upper and lower bounds on variances, as well as higher central moments, of cost accumulators. To overcome the challenges of higher-moment analysis, it generalizes analyses for expectations with an algebraic abstraction that simultaneously analyzes different moments, utilizing relations between them. A key innovation is the notion of moment-polymorphic recursion, and a practical derivation system that handles recursive functions. The analysis has been implemented using a template-based technique that reduces the inference of polynomial bounds to linear programming. Experiments with our prototype central-moment analyzer show that, despite the analyzer's upper/lower bounds on various quantities, it obtains tighter tail bounds than an existing system that uses only raw moments, such as expectations.

These bounds can be obtained through concentration inequalities, which depend on the moments of a distribution, including the expectation (first raw moment) and the variance (second central moment). Tail bounds derived from central moments are generally tighter than those derived from raw moments, although the automated analysis of central moments presents greater difficulty. This paper introduces an analysis method for probabilistic programs that automatically computes symbolic upper and lower bounds on variances and higher central moments of cost accumulators. To address the challenges associated with higher-moment analysis, the method extends existing analyses for expectations by employing an algebraic abstraction that simultaneously examines multiple moments and leverages their interrelations. A key innovation is the concept of moment-polymorphic recursion, along with a practical derivation system for handling recursive functions. The analysis has been implemented using a template-based approach that reduces the inference of polynomial bounds to linear programming. Experimental results with the prototype central-moment analyzer demonstrate that, despite the bounds on various quantities, it achieves tighter tail bounds compared to an existing system that relies solely on raw moments, such as expectations.

The book is called *The Ordeal of Richard Feverel* by George Meredith, published in 1905. It has many chapters. The first is titled *The Inmates of Raynham Abbey*. The next is *Juvenile Stratagems*. Then *Daphne's Bower*. The chapter after that is *The Bitter Cup*. Then *A Fine Distinction*. The next is *Richard Passes Through His Preliminary Ordeal*. Then *The Last Act of the Bakewell Comedy Is Closed in a Letter*. The next chapter is *The Blossoming Season*. Then *The Magnetic Age*. The next is *An Attraction*. Then *Ferdinand and Miranda*. The following chapter is *Unmasking of Master Ripton Thompson*. Then *Good Wine and Good Blood*. The next is *The System Encounters the Wild Oats Special Plea*. Then *A Diversion Played on a Penny Whistle*. The next chapter is *Celebrates the Time-Honoured Treatment of a Dragon by the Hero*. Then *Richard Is Summoned to Town to Hear a Sermon*. The next is *Indicates the Approaches of Fever*. Then *Crisis in the Apple-Disease*. The following chapter is *Of the Spring Primrose and the Autumnal*. Then *In Which the Hero Takes a Step*. The next is *Records the Rapid Development of the Hero*. Then *Contains an Intercession for the Heroine*. The next chapter is *Preparations for Action Were Conducted Under the April of Lovers*. Then *The Last Act of the Comedy Takes the Place of the First*. The next is *Celebrates the Breakfast*. Then *The Philosopher Appears in Person*. The next chapter is *Procession of the Cake*. Then *Nursing the Devil*. The following is *Conquest of an Epicure*. Then *Clare's Marriage*. The next chapter is *A Dinner-Party at Richmond*. Then *Mrs. Berry on Matrimony*. The next is *An Enchantress*. Then *The Little Bird and the Falcon: A Berry to the Rescue!*. The following chapter is *Clare's Diary*. Then *Austin Returns*. The next is *Nature Speaks*. The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, by George Meredith, 1905—its pages are a labyrinth of names, each one a whisper of fate, each chapter a pulse in the great, beating heart of destiny. I. The Inmates of Raynham Abbey—where shadows dance and secrets slumber. II. Fates selected the fourteenth birthday to try the strength, as if the world itself were a crucible, and Richard its molten core. III. The Magian Conflict—where minds clash like hammers on anvil, and the air hums with the tension of a storm about to break. IV. Arson—flames licking the edges of the soul, testing what remains when the world burns. V. Adrian plies his hook, a fisherman of dreams, casting lines into the deep where only the bold dare to dive. VI. Juvenile Stratagems—youth’s rebellion, a dance of wit and will, where every move is a gamble on the edge of a blade. VII. Daphne’s Bower—where innocence blooms and the world holds its breath. VIII. The Bitter Cup—poisoned by fate, yet drunk with the promise of transformation. IX. A Fine Distinction—between the seen and the unseen, the real and the imagined, the soul and the shadow. X. Richard passes through his preliminary ordeal, a rite of passage where the self is both judge and jury. XI. The Last Act of the Bakewell Comedy is Closed in a Letter—where words become weapons, and silence speaks louder than a thousand screams. XII. The Blossoming Season—spring’s breath on the skin, a promise of renewal. XIII. The Magnetic Age—where the unseen pulls the seen, and the heart is a compass lost in the storm. XIV. An Attraction—love, lust, and the pull of the unknown, all converging in a single, fateful moment. XV. Ferdinand and Miranda—two souls entwined, their story a mirror to the world’s own. XVI. Unmasking of Master Ripton Thompson—where truth peels back the layers like a flower in bloom. XVII. Good Wine and Good Blood—where the past and present collide, and the future is a glass half full. XVIII. The System Encounters the Wild Oats—where order meets chaos, and the world is remade. XIX. A Diversion Played on a Penny Whistle—where the absurd becomes the sublime, and laughter is the only weapon. XX. Celebrates the Time-Honoured Treatment of a Dragon by the Hero—where courage is tested, and the world is made anew. XXI. Richard is Summoned to Town to Hear a Sermon—where the voice of the church meets the voice of the soul. XXII. Indicates the Approaches of Fever—where the body betrays the mind, and the spirit is left in the dark. XXIII. Crisis in the Apple-Disease—where decay and decay are the only truths. XXIV. Of the Spring Primrose and the Autumnal—where time is a wheel, and all things must return. XXV. In Which the Hero Takes a Step—forward, backward, or sideways, the path is never clear. XXVI. Captain Duff of the sloop "Fancy" had a tough time. Then came an unlucky smash. People called them "Chinks" and "Dope." There were smugglers in Puget Sound. Things got very trying. A lesson in kedging was learned. A mysterious light was chased. Bonny made an invention that worked. They were captured by a revenue-cutter. The first mate and crew escaped. A little Siwash kid saved them. Life was in Skookum John's camp. A treacherous Indian from Neah Bay showed up. An exciting race for liberty happened. A case of mistaken identity was had. Two short but exciting voyages were taken. Alaric Todd had his darkest hour. Phil Ryder paid a debt. Alaric was engaged to interpret for the French. Preparing for an ascent was done. Bonny commanded the situation. On the edge of Paradise Valley they were. Mount Rainier was placed underfoot. Blown from the rim of a crater they were. A desperate situation arose. A song saved Alaric's life. Laid up for repairs they were. Chased by a madman they were. A gang of friendly loggers came. In a Northwest logging camp they were. What is a hump-durgin? Alaric and Bonny took to flight again. Bonny discovered his friend the tramp. A flood of light was seen. Illustrations showed the ice above Gibraltar. Alaric made his first decision. "Vell, I tell you; I givs twenty-five." Bonny's invention started the arrival at Skookum John's. Bonny seized a truck, and Alaric a mattress. "Bonny was jerked backward." "They were paralyzed with terror." Rick Dale.

O sovereigns, dominators, and architects of dominion across the expanse of realms, is this the testament you offer to the divine—this grotesque abomination, this entity bent and extinguished of spirit? How shall you ever rectify this form—reclaim it from the abyss, rekindle its gaze toward the heavens, restore the luminous essence and the harmonious dream? How shall you mend the ancient wounds, the treacherous betrayals, the irreparable sorrows? O sovereigns, dominators, and architects of dominion, how will posterity judge this man? How shall you answer his unyielding inquiry in that moment when tempests of upheaval convulse the world? How shall the kingdoms and their kings—those who molded him into this being—stand before the judgment of eternity, when this voiceless horror shall speak to the divine after the long silence of ages?

But the real historic strength of England, physical and moral, has never had anything to do with this athletic specialism; it has been rather hindered by it. Somebody said that the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton playing-fields. It was a particularly unfortunate remark, for the English contribution to the victory of Waterloo depended very much more than is common in victories upon the steadiness of the rank and file in an almost desperate situation. The Battle of Waterloo was won by the stubbornness of the common soldier—that is to say, it was won by the man who had never been to Eton. It was absurd to say that Waterloo was won on Eton cricket-fields. But it might have been fairly said that Waterloo was won on the village green, where clumsy boys played a very clumsy cricket. In a word, it was the average of the nation that was strong, and athletic glories do not indicate much about the average of a nation. Waterloo was not won by good cricket-players. But Waterloo was won by bad cricket-players, by a mass of men who had some minimum of athletic instincts and habits. It is a good sign in a nation when such things are done badly. The enduring vitality of England—both corporeal and ethical—has never aligned with the narrow domain of athletic prowess; rather, it has been obstructed by it. A remark once made—that the Battle of Waterloo was won on Eton playing-fields—was not merely inapt, but profoundly misleading. The English role in securing that victory rested far more upon the steadfastness of ordinary soldiers in dire circumstances than is typically the case in such triumphs. The Battle of Waterloo was not won by the refined dexterity of the elite, but by the unyielding resolve of the common man, the individual who had never set foot in Eton. To claim that Waterloo was won on Eton cricket-fields is to commit a rhetorical absurdity. Yet, one might reasonably argue that it was won on the village green, where awkward youths engaged in an equally awkward game. In essence, it was the collective average of the nation that proved decisive, and athletic excellence offers little insight into the character of the masses. Waterloo was not secured by skilled cricketers, but by those who played the game poorly—by a multitude of men possessing only a rudimentary grasp of physical discipline. It is a positive sign for a nation when such activities are performed inadequately, for it signals widespread participation. Conversely, when such endeavors are executed with precision, it reveals a narrow segment of society engaged in them, while the rest of the populace remains passive. Were we to encounter in England only accounts of walking at forty-five miles daily without fatigue, we might conclude that only a few individuals walked at all, while the majority were transported in comfort. But if walking is described as slow, laborious, and often exhausting, we may infer that the bulk of the population remains active, that England is still, in a literal sense, on its feet.

Neither make too much of flaws and occasional overstatements. Some persons seem to think that absolute truth, in the form of rigidly stated propositions, is all that conversation admits. This is precisely as if a musician should insist on having nothing but perfect chords and simple melodies,—no diminished fifths, no flat sevenths, no flourishes, on any account. Now it is fair to say, that, just as music must have all these, so conversation must have its partial truths, its embellished truths, its exaggerated truths. It is in its higher forms an artistic product, and admits the ideal element as much as pictures or statues. One man who is a little too literal can spoil the talk of a whole tableful of men of *esprit*.—"Yes," you say, "but who wants to hear fanciful people's nonsense? Put the facts to it, and then see where it is!"—Certainly, if a man is too fond of paradox,—if he is flighty and empty,—if, instead of striking those fifths and sevenths, those harmonious discords, often so much better than the twinned octaves, in the music of thought,—if, instead of striking these, he jangles the chords, stick a fact into him like a stiletto. But remember that talking is one of the fine arts,—the noblest, the most important, and the most difficult,—and that its fluent harmonies may be spoiled by the intrusion of a single harsh note. Therefore conversation which is suggestive rather than argumentative, which lets out the most of each talker's results of thought, is commonly the pleasantest and the most profitable. It is not easy, at the best, for two persons talking together to make the most of each other's thoughts, there are so many of them.

Neither should one exaggerate the significance of flaws or occasional hyperbole. Some individuals appear to believe that conversation is confined to the realm of absolute truth, expressed through rigidly formulated propositions. This notion is akin to a musician who insists solely on perfect chords and uncomplicated melodies—excluding diminished fifths, flat sevenths, and embellishments altogether. Yet, just as music thrives on such elements, so too does discourse require partial truths, embellished truths, and even exaggerated truths. In its most elevated form, conversation is an artistic endeavor, embracing the ideal as fully as painting or sculpture. A single individual overly literal in his interpretations can disrupt the intellectual harmony of an entire gathering of men of *esprit*.—"Yes," you may argue, "but who desires to hear the absurdities of fanciful minds? Let us put facts to the test, and we shall see!"—Certainly, if a person is excessively fond of paradox, if he is frivolous and vacuous, if he substitutes jarring dissonance for the harmonious discord that often surpasses the simplicity of consonant octaves in the architecture of thought, then a sharp fact should be thrust upon him like a stiletto.
