Then there are the sentimentalists, who are the largest class and who make the easiest work of social questions. In the study of the individual organism we know that normal physiology presents the greatest difficulties and is the essential basis for a correct study of diseases and remedies. We also know that popular knowledge of physiology is meager in the extreme, while popular notions attach almost entirely to diseases and to remedies. The same is true of society. The study of the structure and functions of the organs of society is long and difficult, and we have, as yet, accomplished very little towards it. We can hope to accomplish much only by a long study of history and a careful examination of institutions. I venture to say that no study except the highest mathematics has ever yet made such demands on the human mind as are made by sociology. We cannot make an experiment in sociology because we cannot dispose of the time, that is, of the lives of a body of men and women. We have to carry in mind a great number of variables, to weigh their value, and to deduce their resultant, although for many of them we can find no unit of measurement or comparison, and although we have no notation to help us. I think that we shall have to adopt some of these methods of the other sciences sooner or later, but at present I see no means of advancing sociology save by the cultivation of a trained judgment through the careful study of sociological phenomena and sequences.

There exist a significant number of sentimentalists, who constitute the largest group and find social issues relatively straightforward. In the examination of the individual organism, it is evident that normal physiology is the most challenging domain and forms the foundational basis for the accurate study of diseases and their treatments. Similarly, common understanding of physiology is exceedingly limited, with public perception predominantly focused on diseases and their remedies. This pattern is mirrored in society. The analysis of the structure and functions of societal organs is complex and demanding, and to date, progress in this area has been minimal. Substantial advancement can be anticipated only through extensive historical study and meticulous scrutiny of institutions. I assert that no field of study, apart from the most advanced mathematics, has ever imposed such rigorous intellectual demands as sociology. Conducting experiments in sociology is impractical due to the inability to manipulate the time span encompassing the lives of individuals. A multitude of variables must be considered, evaluated, and their combined effects determined, despite the absence of standardized units for many of these variables and the lack of systematic notation. While I believe that some methodologies from other scientific disciplines will eventually be adopted, at present, the only viable path for advancing sociology lies in the development of a well-trained judgment through the thorough investigation of sociological phenomena and their sequences.

Then there are the sentimentalists—those soft-hearted scribes of society—who number in the millions and who treat the tangled web of human relations with the ease of a child playing with clay. In the anatomy of the individual, we find that the healthy body, with its seamless rhythms and quiet strength, is the hardest to grasp, yet it is the very foundation upon which all illness and cure depend. The same is true of society: the structure and function of its organs—its institutions, its customs, its unseen mechanisms—are as complex and elusive as the human heart. Popular understanding, like a flickering candle in the dark, shines brightest on the dramatic, the broken, the miraculous. Yet the true work of understanding lies in the quiet, the unseen, the vast and intricate machinery of the social body. We have barely begun to scratch the surface. To move forward, we must immerse ourselves in the slow, patient study of history, of institutions, of the silent dance of human interaction. Sociology, that stubborn and demanding sister of science, asks more of the mind than even mathematics, which has long been the queen of abstraction. We cannot run experiments here, for time is not a tool we can bend to our will. We must watch, weigh, and wonder—though often without a compass or a map. And so, we must train our judgment, not with haste, but with care, through the careful study of the world as it is.

I assert that no field of study, apart from the most advanced mathematics, has ever imposed such rigorous intellectual demands as sociology. Conducting experiments in sociology is impractical due to the inability to manipulate the time span encompassing the lives of individuals. A multitude of variables must be considered, evaluated, and their combined effects determined, despite the absence of standardized units for many of these variables and the lack of systematic notation. While I believe that some methodologies from other scientific disciplines will eventually be adopted, at present, the only viable path for advancing sociology lies in the development of a well-trained judgment through the thorough investigation of sociological phenomena and their sequences.

There are a lot of people who feel strongly about emotions and feelings, and they're the biggest group. They find it easy to talk about problems in society. When we look at the body, it's hard to understand how it works normally, but that's important because it helps us understand sickness and how to treat it. People don't know much about how the body works, but they know a lot about illness and what to do about it. The same is true for society. Understanding how society works and what it does is hard and we haven't done much of it yet. We need to study history and look closely at how things are organized. I think sociology is harder than any other subject except math. You can't do experiments in sociology because you can't control people's lives. You have to think about a lot of things at once, weigh them, and try to figure out what happens. But some of these things can't be measured, and there's no clear way to write them down. I think we'll have to use some of the methods from other sciences, but right now, the only way to move forward is to study carefully and develop good judgment about how society works and what happens next.

Then there exist the sentimentalists, a predominant faction whose facile engagement with social matters belies the complexity of the subject. In the domain of the individual organism, we recognize that normal physiology, though foundational to understanding pathology and treatment, remains an arduous field of inquiry, its intricacies often obscured by the populace’s preoccupation with illness and cure. Analogously, society’s structural and functional mechanisms—its organs, so to speak—elude comprehensive analysis, their study demanding both temporal depth and intellectual rigor. To date, our grasp of these mechanisms remains embryonic, reliant upon historical scrutiny and institutional examination as the principal avenues of progress. Sociology, in its demand for abstract reasoning and meticulous observation, surpasses even the most demanding branches of mathematics in its cognitive toll. Unlike the laboratory, where controlled variables yield quantifiable results, sociology operates within a realm where variables are legion, their interplay elusive, and their measurement imprecise. The absence of standardized metrics or notation further complicates this endeavor. While the adoption of methodologies from other disciplines may eventually prove indispensable, the immediate path forward lies in the refinement of judgment through sustained engagement with sociological phenomena and their sequels.

Then there are the sentimentalists—those soft-hearted scribes of society—who number in the millions and who treat the tangled web of human relations with the ease of a child playing with clay. In the anatomy of the individual, we find that the healthy body, with its seamless rhythms and quiet strength, is the hardest to grasp, yet it is the very foundation upon which all illness and cure depend. The same is true of society: the structure and function of its organs—its institutions, its customs, its unseen mechanisms—are as complex and elusive as the human heart. Popular understanding, like a flickering candle in the dark, shines brightest on the dramatic, the broken, the miraculous. Yet the true work of understanding lies in the quiet, the unseen, the vast and intricate machinery of the social body. We have barely begun to scratch the surface. To move forward, we must immerse ourselves in the slow, patient study of history, of institutions, of the silent dance of human interaction. Sociology, that stubborn and demanding sister of science, asks more of the mind than even mathematics, which has long been the queen of abstraction. We cannot run experiments here, for time is not a tool we can bend to our will. We must watch, weigh, and wonder—though often without a compass or a map. And so, we must train our judgment, not with haste, but with care, through the careful study of the world as it is.

President Lincoln in a note to Mayor Ramsey once wrote: "The lady bearer of this note says she has two sons who want to work. Set them at it if possible. Wanting work is so rare a want that it should be encouraged." A college officer in my position at the opening of the college year would not be inclined to agree with Mr. Lincoln, for half the correspondence which comes to my desk during the summer months has to do with men who either want to work, or who say they do, in order that they may defray their college expenses. There are so many of them that their correspondence becomes almost depressing at times, for I realize the disappointments and the difficulties which very many of these boys will encounter after they reach college, and their unfitness to do any definite work well. "I have been out of high school three years," one young fellow writes, "and have not been able to save any money. I want, however, very much to go to college. Can you secure a place for me to work where I can earn my board and room and such extra money as I shall need for my other small expenses?" This man, who has given all his time to work for three years and who has done nothing more than live, expects easily to carry a college course which in itself requires most of a man's time to do justice to, and at the same time to earn his living on the side. I get many such letters from those who feel that earning one's living and going to college are in no way incompatible. So much has been written about the fellows who have started to college without a cent and who have later been valedictorians of their classes and ultimately President of the United States, or at least a member of his cabinet, that the average high school boy has little conception of what sacrifice and deprivation such a procedure involves; if he did understand he would nat so often undertake it, or he would do so after more careful deliberation.

If he were to comprehend the nature of these sacrifices, he would be less likely to pursue this path without careful consideration.

President Lincoln, in a note to Mayor Ramsey, once wrote: "The lady bearer of this note says she has two sons who want to work. Set them at it if possible. Wanting work is so rare a want that it should be encouraged." A college officer, standing at the threshold of the academic year, would likely scoff at such sentiment. The summer months bring a flood of letters—each one a plea, a promise, a desperate hope—that men seek work, or claim to seek work, to pay for their education. These letters, so many and so heavy with longing, weigh on me like a storm before the rain. I see in them the shadows of disappointment, the silent struggles of boys who, once in college, will find themselves unprepared for the weight of real labor. One young man writes: "I've been out of high school for three years, and I've saved nothing. I want to go to college very much. Can you find me a place to work where I can earn my board, room, and a little more for my other expenses?" This man, who has spent three years surviving on the edge of existence, now expects to juggle a college course with the demands of a job. I receive countless such letters from those who believe earning a living and attending college can coexist, as if the two were mere sides of the same coin. Yet the stories of those who started college with nothing and later rose to greatness—valedictorians, presidents, cabinet members—are often told as if they were miracles, not the result of sacrifice and deprivation. If only the average high school boy understood the cost, he would hesitate, and perhaps, choose more wisely.

Wanting work is so rare a want that it should be encouraged." A college officer, in the early days of the academic year, would likely find themselves in disagreement with Mr. Lincoln’s sentiment, for the bulk of correspondence received during the summer months pertains to individuals—predominantly young men—who either express a desire to work or claim to do so, in the hope of alleviating the costs associated with their college education. The sheer volume of such letters has, at times, grown wearying, as I am compelled to confront the realities of the challenges and inadequacies these young men will inevitably face upon entering the academic environment. One such correspondent writes: "I have been out of high school for three years and have not managed to save a single penny. I wish, however, to pursue higher education. Can you procure me a position where I may earn my board and lodging, as well as additional funds for incidental expenses?" This individual, who has devoted three years solely to labor and subsistence, anticipates with ease the dual burden of sustaining a college curriculum and earning a livelihood. I receive numerous such missives from those who perceive no fundamental contradiction between the pursuit of education and the necessity of labor. The widespread narrative surrounding those who entered college with nothing and later achieved academic distinction, even ascending to the presidency or cabinet, has obscured the profound sacrifices and privations such a path entails. Were these realities more fully understood, the average high school student would likely approach such a decision with greater caution, or only after more deliberate consideration.

President Lincoln, in a note to Mayor Ramsey, once wrote: "The lady bearer of this note says she has two sons who want to work. Set them at it if possible. Wanting work is so rare a want that it should be encouraged." A college officer, standing at the threshold of the academic year, would likely scoff at such sentiment. The summer months bring a flood of letters—each one a plea, a promise, a desperate hope—that men seek work, or claim to seek work, to pay for their education. These letters, so many and so heavy with longing, weigh on me like a storm before the rain. I see in them the shadows of disappointment, the silent struggles of boys who, once in college, will find themselves unprepared for the weight of real labor. One young man writes: "I've been out of high school for three years, and I've saved nothing. I want to go to college very much. Can you find me a place to work where I can earn my board, room, and a little more for my other expenses?" This man, who has spent three years surviving on the edge of existence, now expects to juggle a college course with the demands of a job. I receive countless such letters from those who believe earning a living and attending college can coexist, as if the two were mere sides of the same coin. Yet the stories of those who started college with nothing and later rose to greatness—valedictorians, presidents, cabinet members—are often told as if they were miracles, not the result of sacrifice and deprivation. If only the average high school boy understood the cost, he would hesitate, and perhaps, choose more wisely.

But, although palæontology is a comparatively youthful scientific speciality, the mass of materials with which it has to deal is already prodigious. In the last fifty years the number of known fossil remains of invertebrated animals has been trebled or quadrupled. The work of interpretation of vertebrate fossils, the foundations of which were so solidly laid by Cuvier, was carried on, with wonderful vigour and success, by Agassiz in Switzerland, by Von Meyer in Germany, and last, but not least, by Owen in this country, while, in later years, a multitude of workers have laboured in the same field. In many groups of the animal kingdom the number of fossil forms already known is as great as that of the existing species. In some cases it is much greater; and there are entire orders of animals of the existence of which we should know nothing except for the evidence afforded by fossil remains. With all this it may be safely assumed that, at the present moment, we are not acquainted with a tithe of the fossils which will sooner or later be discovered. If we may judge by the profusion yielded within the last few years by the Tertiary formations of North America, there seems to be no limit to the multitude of Mammalian remains to be expected from that continent; and analogy leads us to expect similar riches in Eastern Asia, whenever the Tertiary formations of that region are as carefully explored. Again, we have as yet almost everything to learn respecting the terrestrial population of the Mesozoic epoch—and it seems as if the Western territories of the United States were about to prove as instructive in regard to this point as they have in respect of tertiary life. My friend Professor Marsh informs me that, within two years, remains of more than 160 distinct individuals of mammals, belonging to twenty species and nine genera, have been found in a space not larger than the floor of a good-sized room; while beds of the same age have yielded 300 reptiles, varying in size from a length of 60 feet or 80 feet to the dimensions of a rabbit.

The work of interpreting vertebrate fossils, which Cuvier laid the groundwork for, has been carried on with astonishing vigor by Agassiz in Switzerland, Von Meyer in Germany, and Owen here in England. And then there’s the whole swarm of workers who’ve since joined the fray. In many animal groups, the number of known fossils is equal to the number of living species. In some cases, it’s even more. Entire orders of animals would be unknown to us if not for these fossil clues. And yet, we’ve barely scratched the surface. If we judge by the bounty from North America’s Tertiary formations in recent years, there’s no end to the mammals yet to be unearthed. And if the same logic holds, Eastern Asia will soon reveal its own treasure trove. As for the Mesozoic era’s land animals—there’s still so much to learn. The American West, which has given us so much about the Tertiary, may yet give us even more about the Mesozoic. My friend Professor Marsh tells me that in just two years, more than 160 distinct mammal individuals—spanning twenty species and nine genera—have been found in a space no bigger than a large room’s floor. And in beds of the same age, 300 reptiles have been uncovered, some stretching over 60 or 80 feet long, others no bigger than a rabbit.

Cross-examined.—I am an officer in the Grenadier Guards. I have had some experience of stage-plays. I believe that nothing is easier than to write a good stage-play. I have written one myself. I found it extremely easy. Mounting guard was an intellectual exercise not to be mentioned in the same breath with it. My play has not been produced—not yet. I have shown it to several managers—they hesitate to produce it, on the ground that it is too intellectual. I had no objection to bring it down to the comprehension of the audience; but I did not see any way of making it less intellectual than it was—I have no objection to state its name—it is a burlesque called *Tom Tiddler.*

Whatever was once the custom, in these days, at least, fraternity men are expected to pay their debts and to do so promptly. The young man with the buoyancy and optimism of Mr. Skimpole, in *[Bleak House](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bleak_House),* who held that "the sordid word money should never be mentioned in the relations of friendship" is having little vogue at the present time. The enthusiastic life insurance agent, if you will admit his logic, can prove to you that if you will pay your premiums long enough they will cost you nothing, but every sensible man knows that the thing that is worth anything costs something, and the fraternity is no exception. Fraternity men in the past have too frequently taken their obligations lightly, and so in a financial way have brought fraternities into disrepute. Fraternity officers have begun strongly to emphasize the importance of financial matters in the fraternity and are insisting upon the introduction of accounting systems into all chapters which will make it possible for fraternity accounts to be kept accurately and which will impress upon the fraternity man from the outset his obligation to meet his bills when they are due. When a boy goes into a fraternity, neither he nor his father should be deceived as to the actual cost of membership, nor allowed to believe that payment may be evaded or deferred. It is ordinarily as unwise to go into a fraternity with the idea that the cost of living will thus be reduced as it is to enter matrimony with the thought that it will cost no more to support a family than an individual. With us at the University of Illinois the fraternity man is likely to be called upon to expend twenty per cent more than if he had remained outside of the organization, and if he develops popularity and contracts the joining habit, it may cost him considerably more than this.

Fraternity members today are expected to fulfill their financial obligations in a timely manner. The ideal of a young man, such as Mr. Skimpole from *Bleak House*, who believed that the term "money" should never be mentioned in friendship, is no longer widely accepted. A life insurance agent may argue that paying premiums over time results in no net cost, yet any reasonable person understands that value requires cost, and this principle applies to fraternity membership as well. Historically, fraternity members have often neglected their financial responsibilities, leading to a negative perception of fraternities. In response, fraternity officers have placed greater emphasis on financial accountability, requiring the implementation of accounting systems within each chapter. These systems aim to ensure accurate record-keeping and to instill from the beginning the responsibility of meeting financial obligations as they become due. When a student joins a fraternity, neither he nor his parents should be misled regarding the true cost of membership, nor should they believe that payments can be avoided or postponed. It is as imprudent to enter a fraternity expecting reduced living expenses as it is to enter marriage believing that supporting a family will cost no more than supporting oneself. At the University of Illinois, fraternity members typically incur expenses 20 percent higher than those who remain outside the organization. If a student gains popularity and becomes involved in the fraternity, the financial burden may significantly exceed this amount.

The modern fraternity man is no longer a romantic figure draped in the haze of idealism, but a man of accounts, a ledger of promises and payments. Once, there were those—like Mr. Skimpole, that buoyant soul in *Bleak House*—who believed the word "money" should never be spoken in the language of friendship. But those days are gone, swept away by the sharp winds of reality. Today, the young man who thinks he can live without paying his debts is a fool, a man who has not yet learned that the world is not a place of miracles, but of obligations. The life insurance agent, with his glossy logic, may whisper sweet lies about premiums vanishing into nothing, but every sensible man knows that anything worth having costs something. And the fraternity, that sacred bond, is no exception. In the past, fraternity men treated their promises like dust, and in doing so, they sullied the very institutions they swore to uphold. Now, the officers have begun to tighten the reins, demanding that chapters adopt systems of accounting, that every dollar spent be tracked, that every promise be honored. When a boy steps into a fraternity, neither he nor his father should be misled about the true cost, nor allowed to believe that debts can be postponed or ignored. It is as foolish to think a fraternity will reduce your expenses as it is to believe marriage will cost no more than living alone. At the University of Illinois, the fraternity man is likely to spend twenty percent more than the man who stays outside, and if he grows popular, if he contracts the habit of joining, the cost may rise far beyond that.

In contemporary society, the once-cherished ideal of fraternity life is increasingly subsumed by a pragmatic imperative: the obligation to settle debts with punctuality. In response, fraternity leadership has initiated a rigorous recalibration, emphasizing fiscal responsibility through the implementation of structured accounting systems across all chapters. Entry into fraternity life should not be shrouded in illusions of economic benefit; neither the initiate nor his progenitor should be misled into believing that financial obligations can be deferred or evaded. This is as ill-advised as the notion that matrimony entails no additional financial burden. At the University of Illinois, the fraternity member is typically expected to bear an additional twenty percent in expenses compared to his non-fraternity counterpart, and should he cultivate popularity and the compulsion to join, the financial toll may escalate significantly beyond this threshold.

The idealistic youth, reminiscent of Mr. Skimpole from *Bleak House*, who once maintained that the sordid term "money" should be banished from the lexicon of friendship, now finds himself an anachronism. The life insurance agent, with his calculated logic, may persuade one that prolonged payments render cost null, yet the discerning individual recognizes that value is inseparable from sacrifice—fraternity, like any other institution, is no exception. Historically, fraternity members have often approached financial commitments with levity, thereby sowing the seeds of disrepute within their organizations. In response, fraternity leadership has initiated a rigorous recalibration, emphasizing fiscal responsibility through the implementation of structured accounting systems across all chapters. These systems aim not merely to track expenditures but to instill from the outset a profound awareness of one's duty to honor obligations upon their due. Entry into fraternity life should not be shrouded in illusions of economic benefit; neither the initiate nor his progenitor should be misled into believing that financial obligations can be deferred or evaded. This is as ill-advised as the notion that matrimony entails no additional financial burden. At the University of Illinois, the fraternity member is typically expected to bear an additional twenty percent in expenses compared to his non-fraternity counterpart, and should he cultivate popularity and the compulsion to join, the financial toll may escalate significantly beyond this threshold.

The modern fraternity man is no longer a romantic figure draped in the haze of idealism, but a man of accounts, a ledger of promises and payments. Once, there were those—like Mr. Skimpole, that buoyant soul in *Bleak House*—who believed the word "money" should never be spoken in the language of friendship. But those days are gone, swept away by the sharp winds of reality. Today, the young man who thinks he can live without paying his debts is a fool, a man who has not yet learned that the world is not a place of miracles, but of obligations. The life insurance agent, with his glossy logic, may whisper sweet lies about premiums vanishing into nothing, but every sensible man knows that anything worth having costs something. And the fraternity, that sacred bond, is no exception. In the past, fraternity men treated their promises like dust, and in doing so, they sullied the very institutions they swore to uphold. Now, the officers have begun to tighten the reins, demanding that chapters adopt systems of accounting, that every dollar spent be tracked, that every promise be honored. When a boy steps into a fraternity, neither he nor his father should be misled about the true cost, nor allowed to believe that debts can be postponed or ignored. It is as foolish to think a fraternity will reduce your expenses as it is to believe marriage will cost no more than living alone. At the University of Illinois, the fraternity man is likely to spend twenty percent more than the man who stays outside, and if he grows popular, if he contracts the habit of joining, the cost may rise far beyond that.

Merited and timely as such criticism may appear to a transient observer of the State university, it is recognized as superficial and essentially false by all those who have felt the inner throb and glow of the enterprise. Idealist the institution is not, if idealism means a sterile yearning for the unattainable. Materialist it is not, if materialism is identified with satisfaction in the welfare of the senses. The State university to-day is at the same time intensely visionary and intensely practical: its driving power is the creative artist's desire to externalize and eternize his dream. With eyes fixed upon that end, it does not shrink from the coarse tasks of mixing pigments, quarrying stone, or melting bronze. It would honor every truth by use, and it holds that the triumph of the spiritual is the subjugation of the material. The financial support which it solicits is the means to the realization of a vision embracing almost the whole of life, and the wealth which it helps to create is but the first fruits of its contemplated harvest.

The enduring renown of our most distinguished comic dramatist rests exclusively or predominantly upon but three of his five theatrical works. His inaugural comedy serves merely as a dazzling imitation, a study in homage to predecessors whose own brilliance had already been eclipsed by this early act of replication. Tragedy, when subjected to his touch, emerges as a grotesque parody, its dignity marred by the artificiality of Lady Wishfort’s affectations. Yet these three comedies alone are sufficient to secure a legacy as enduring as the language itself. Without them, we would possess no exemplars of comedy in its most refined and transcendent form. Ben Jonson, the sole figure who sought to impose order upon the chaotic fusion of genres prevalent in his era—where comedy and tragedy were as inseparable as fate and fortune—failed to infuse his grand, intricate compositions with the natural ease and grace that define authentic comic expression. Among his contemporaries, those who endeavoured to construct a new English comedy upon French ideals, Wycherley proved too crude and Etherege too delicate to rival his achievements; no other alternative existed save the unpolished, unrefined output of Shadwell’s blunt and boisterous genius. Drawing upon Landor’s metaphor, we might assert that a single limb from Molière would have been enough to forge a Congreve, and a limb from Congreve would have sufficed to shape a Sheridan. The robust and forthright wit of Vanbrugh’s comedies secures him a place among the masters, his work a testament to the vitality of a genre in flux.

The fame of our greatest comic dramatist rests mostly on three of his five plays. His first comedy was more of a clever imitation of earlier works, which had already been surpassed by this new effort. His tragedies, on the other hand, feel old and fake, like Lady Wishfort in all her makeup and fuss. But his three great comedies are enough to build a lasting reputation, just like our language. Without these plays, we would have nothing to show of comedy at its best.  

Ben Jonson was the only one who tried to bring real comedy into a time when plays mixed tragedy and comedy like life itself. But he never quite got the natural feel and charm of real comedy into his big, fancy plays. Among those who came before Congreve, trying to build a new kind of English comedy on French ideas, Wycherley was too rough and Etherege too weak. No one else had anything better than Shadwell's rough and clumsy style.  

Using a metaphor from Landor, we can say that a part of Molière would have made a Congreve, and a part of Congreve would have made a Sheridan. Vanbrugh's comedies, with their strong and hearty humor, deserve a place among the best.

The glory of our greatest comic dramatist rests on but three of his five plays—each a spark in the dark, a flicker in the fog. His first comedy, a dazzling imitation of those who had come before, was nothing more than a ghost in the hall, a shadow cast by giants. Tragedy, under his hand, became a caricature, a Lady Wishfort in rouge and ruffles, all pretense and no substance. Yet these three comedies—bold, bright, and brimming with life—sustain a reputation as enduring as the language itself. Without them, we would be left in the dark, with no glimpse of comedy’s purest essence.  

Ben Jonson, that lone reformer, tried to carve a new path through the mire of Elizabethan chaos, but his work, though grand, lacked the lightness, the grace, that comedy demands. His tragedies were heavy, his comedies too stiff, like a man trying to dance in armor. The reputation of our most distinguished comic dramatist rests primarily on three of his five plays. His initial comedy served mainly as a refined imitation of earlier works that had already been rendered obsolete by this early effort of his imitator. Tragedy, when handled by him, appears artificially aged, as if adorned with the patches and cosmetics of Lady Wishfort. Nevertheless, his three major comedies are sufficient to establish a lasting legacy as enduring as the English language itself. Without these, we would lack examples of comedy in its most refined and elevated form. Ben Jonson, the sole figure who sought to introduce comedy through reform during a period when the stage, like life, was a confused mixture of comedy and tragedy, failed to infuse his elaborate and grand work with the natural ease and grace characteristic of comic action and emotion. Among Congreve's immediate predecessors, who aimed to construct a new English comedic tradition upon French foundations, Wycherley's work was too crude, while Etherege's was too delicate to measure against Congreve's. No other playwright of comparable quality existed at the time, save for Shadwell, whose talent was brutish and unrefined. Using a metaphor from Landor, one might say that a single limb from Molière would have been enough to create Congreve, and a limb from Congreve would have been sufficient to create Sheridan. The broad and vigorous humor of Vanbrugh's comedies secures him a place among the masters.

The enduring renown of our most distinguished comic dramatist rests exclusively or predominantly upon but three of his five theatrical works. His inaugural comedy serves merely as a dazzling imitation, a study in homage to predecessors whose own brilliance had already been eclipsed by this early act of replication. Tragedy, when subjected to his touch, emerges as a grotesque parody, its dignity marred by the artificiality of Lady Wishfort’s affectations. Yet these three comedies alone are sufficient to secure a legacy as enduring as the language itself. Without them, we would possess no exemplars of comedy in its most refined and transcendent form. Ben Jonson, the sole figure who sought to impose order upon the chaotic fusion of genres prevalent in his era—where comedy and tragedy were as inseparable as fate and fortune—failed to infuse his grand, intricate compositions with the natural ease and grace that define authentic comic expression. Among his contemporaries, those who endeavoured to construct a new English comedy upon French ideals, Wycherley proved too crude and Etherege too delicate to rival his achievements; no other alternative existed save the unpolished, unrefined output of Shadwell’s blunt and boisterous genius. Drawing upon Landor’s metaphor, we might assert that a single limb from Molière would have been enough to forge a Congreve, and a limb from Congreve would have sufficed to shape a Sheridan. The robust and forthright wit of Vanbrugh’s comedies secures him a place among the masters, his work a testament to the vitality of a genre in flux.

We call it a singular fact, because we Yankees are thought to be fond of the spread-eagle style, and nothing can be more remote from that than his. We are reckoned a practical folks, who would rather hear about a new air-tight stove than about [Plato](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Author:Plato); yet our favorite teacher's practicality is not in the least of the Poor Richard variety. If he have any Buncombe constituency, it is that unrealized commonwealth of philosophers which Plotinus proposed to establish; and if he were to make an almanac, his directions to farmers would be something like this: "October: *Indian Summer;* now is the time to get in your early Vedas." What, then, is his secret? Is it not that he out-Yankees us all? that his range includes us all? that he is equally at home with the potato-disease and original sin, with pegging shoes and the Over-soul? that, as we try all trades, so has he tried all cultures? and above all, that his mysticism gives us a counterpoise to our super-practicality?

We refer to it as a singular fact, not merely for its singular nature, but because it is emblematic of a peculiar dissonance between our self-conception as a people enamored with the broad, sprawling ethos of the spread-eagle and the austere, inward-turned character of this figure. Though we are often cast as a pragmatic people, preferring the utility of an air-tight stove over the abstractions of Plato, our favored teacher’s pragmatism defies the narrow, utilitarian ethos of Poor Richard. His adherents, if any, belong not to the tangible world of common experience but to the unrealized utopia of Plotinus’s philosophical commonwealth. Were he to compile an almanac, his agricultural advice might read: “October: *Indian Summer*; now is the time to gather your early Vedas.” What, then, constitutes his secret? Is it not that he surpasses us in breadth, that his vision encompasses all that we attempt, that he moves with equal ease between the afflictions of the potato and the metaphysical weight of original sin, between the humble pegging shoe and the transcendent Over-soul? That, in essence, he has traversed all cultures as we traverse trades, and that his mysticism serves as a counterbalance to our excess of practicality?

Is it not that he surpasses us in breadth, that his vision encompasses all that we attempt, that he moves with equal ease between the afflictions of the potato and the metaphysical weight of original sin, between the humble pegging shoe and the transcendent Over-soul? That, in essence, he has traversed all cultures as we traverse trades, and that his mysticism serves as a counterbalance to our excess of practicality?

Though we are often cast as a pragmatic people, preferring the utility of an air-tight stove over the abstractions of Plato, our favored teacher’s pragmatism defies the narrow, utilitarian ethos of Poor Richard. We call it a singular fact, for we Yankees pride ourselves on the spread-eagle, the wide-open, the all-American sprawl—yet here he stands, a tightrope walker between the soil and the sublime. We are the practical, the down-to-earth, the ones who’d rather hear about a new air-tight stove than a line from Plato; yet our favorite teacher’s practicality is no mere barnyard wisdom. If he has any following, it’s that phantom commonwealth Plotinus dreamed up, that ghostly republic of thought. The ancient proverb which declares that love is blind is only a half truth: love is only blind of one eye. The expression "blind hate" also contains only a half truth: hate has one powerful eye. When either of these passions is present, it insatiably sets about discovering new objects to feast upon. The lover collects and broods upon the graces of his beloved from the rising of the lark to the going down of the evening star. The husband who thoroughly loses his temper with his wife at the breakfast table busies himself all day long recollecting and amassing all the grievances that he has felt against her during the last ten years; and he returns at night in a sullen rage and with an almost superhuman insight into the deficiencies of his helpmate. So men of letters set out with gusto and find a relish in every wayside berry; or they set out on the satirical foot with a bad taste in their mouths, and for a whole generation occupy themselves with malicious caricatures of their mistress, Life.

The ancient maxim that love is blind reveals a partial truth: it is blind of one eye, while the other remains acutely attuned to the contours of desire. Similarly, the phrase "blind hate" conceals a half-truth, for hate retains a singular, unyielding eye fixed upon its object. When either passion ignites, it becomes an insatiable engine, ceaselessly seeking new sustenance. The lover, in his fevered devotion, gathers the ephemeral graces of his beloved, tracing their arc from the first blush of dawn to the fading light of twilight. The husband, in his tempest of rage, compiles a lifetime of grievances, refining them into a nightmarish clarity that allows him to confront his wife with a grotesque, almost divine insight into her failings. Thus, men of letters, like pilgrims, traverse the terrain of life, either feasting on its wild berries with gusto or, armed with a jaundiced gaze, etching their mistress’s image into the annals of satire for generations.

Love, that one-eyed beast, blinks at the world but fixates on the heart’s dark well. Hate, too, wears a mask—its one eye sharp as a dagger, piercing through the veil of reason. When either passion takes hold, it gnashes its teeth, hunting for new prey to gnaw upon. The lover, with eyes wide as the dawn, chases the fleeting glow of his beloved’s grace, from lark’s first song to the star’s last sigh. The husband, red-faced at breakfast, scours the day for every bruise, every wrong, and returns at dusk with a rage so thick it could drown the moon. Men of letters, too, wander—some with a hunger for the wild, savoring every sour berry; others, with a taste for mockery, carve their mistress’s face into the stone of time, for a generation’s worth of spite. Life, in its infinite folly, is their canvas.

The old saying that love is blind isn't entirely true—love is only blind in one eye. The phrase "blind hate" also isn't fully right—hate has one clear eye. When either of these feelings takes hold, it keeps looking for more to feed on. The lover watches his beloved all day, from morning till night, thinking about her beauty. The husband who gets angry at his wife over breakfast spends the rest of the day remembering all the things he's been upset about for years. He comes home angry and sees more faults in her than ever before. Some people start writing with excitement, finding joy in every little thing. Others start with a grudge, and for years they draw mean pictures of the person they love. Life is like that.

There was a still more pregnant reason for my desertion of the camp of musical criticism. I seemed always to be about ten years ahead of most of the other critics and the orchestral conductors who make out programs. I missed the reviling of Wagner in New York, but I have watched the pundits of the press revile, in turn, Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only, in the end, after their ears, through repeated hearings, had grown accustomed to the new clang-tints, to accept these composers as part of the sacred hierarchy. My orchestral education was carried on under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. Now Thomas was not a great conductor, although he always gave honest musical readings of his scores, but he had one great virtue: he believed that new music should be heard. He performed, therefore, every important European composition as soon as possible after it had been performed abroad. As a result, when I arrived in New York in 1906, having listened to and appraised nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that date, I was amazed to discover that the New York critics were still fighting about these composers, first underpraising them and a little later overpraising them, for Strauss, at any rate, to my mind, has never been a whit superior as a composer to such a man as Liszt. In Paris, in 1913, I heard Stravinsky's [Sacre du Printemps](https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=Sacre_du_Printemps&action=edit&redlink=1) and a good deal more of this Russian's music. I wrote a panegyric about Le Sacre du Printemps in my first book,[[1]](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Red#cite_note-1) published in 1915. In 1924, Le Sacre du Printemps has at last been performed in New York and the critics have at last accepted Stravinsky. So, indeed, apparently, have the conductors who, until the past four years, hardly ever permitted his name to be emblazoned on their programs. The job of music critic in New York, therefore, is certainly not an ideal occupation for a man with imagination and foresight.

I left the world of musical criticism for a reason that went deeper than I first thought. I always felt ahead of most critics and conductors in New York. I missed the angry talk about Wagner, but I saw how the newspapers turned against Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, one after another. At first, they didn’t like them, then they did. But only after they heard them many times did they start to accept them as part of the musical tradition.

I learned about orchestral music under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. He wasn’t a great conductor, but he had one good thing: he believed in hearing new music. He played every important European work as soon as it was performed abroad. So when I came to New York in 1906, I had already heard most of the major works by Strauss and Debussy. I was surprised to find that the critics were still arguing about them. They first didn’t like them, then they praised them too much. In my opinion, Strauss was never better than Liszt.

In 1913, I heard Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps* in Paris. I wrote about it in my first book, published in 1915. It wasn’t until 1924, when the piece was finally played in New York, that the critics and conductors started to take Stravinsky seriously. That’s when they began to include his name on their programs. So, being a music critic in New York isn’t the best job for someone who has imagination and can see what’s coming.

There was a further significant reason for my departure from the camp of musical criticism. I consistently found myself approximately ten years ahead of most critics and orchestral conductors in their assessment of musical works. I had missed the controversy surrounding Wagner in New York, yet I observed the press pundits shift their criticism from Wagner to Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky. Eventually, after repeated exposure, these composers were accepted as part of the established musical canon. My orchestral education was conducted under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. While Thomas was not a great conductor, he consistently provided honest interpretations of the scores he conducted. His most notable quality was his belief in the necessity of hearing new music. As a result, he introduced every significant European composition as soon as it was performed abroad. Consequently, when I arrived in New York in 1906, I had already listened to and evaluated nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that time. I was astonished to find that New York critics were still engaged in debate over these composers, initially undervaluing them and later overvaluing them. In my opinion, Strauss has never been significantly superior as a composer to someone like Liszt. In 1913, I heard Stravinsky's *Sacre du Printemps* and a substantial amount of his other works. I wrote a favorable review of *Sacre du Printemps* in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Sacre du Printemps* had finally been performed in New York, and the critics had finally accepted Stravinsky. Similarly, conductors who had rarely included his name on their programs in the preceding four years had also come to accept him. Therefore, the role of a music critic in New York is not an ideal position for someone with imagination and foresight.

I wrote a favorable review of *Sacre du Printemps* in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Sacre du Printemps* had finally been performed in New York, and the critics had finally accepted Stravinsky. Similarly, conductors who had rarely included his name on their programs in the preceding four years had also come to accept him. Therefore, the role of a music critic in New York is not an ideal position for someone with imagination and foresight.

There was a further significant reason for my departure from the camp of musical criticism. I consistently found myself approximately ten years ahead of most critics and orchestral conductors in their assessment of musical works. I had missed the controversy surrounding Wagner in New York, yet I observed the press pundits shift their criticism from Wagner to Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky. Eventually, after repeated exposure, these composers were accepted as part of the established musical canon. My orchestral education was conducted under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. While Thomas was not a great conductor, he consistently provided honest interpretations of the scores he conducted. His most notable quality was his belief in the necessity of hearing new music. As a result, he introduced every significant European composition as soon as it was performed abroad. Consequently, when I arrived in New York in 1906, I had already listened to and evaluated nearly all the major works of Strauss and Debussy composed up to that time. I left the world of musical criticism for a reason that went deeper than I first thought. I always felt ahead of most critics and conductors in New York. I missed the angry talk about Wagner, but I saw how the newspapers turned against Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, one after another. At first, they didn’t like them, then they did. But only after they heard them many times did they start to accept them as part of the musical tradition.

I learned about orchestral music under Theodore Thomas in Chicago. He wasn’t a great conductor, but he had one good thing: he believed in hearing new music. He played every important European work as soon as it was performed abroad. So when I came to New York in 1906, I had already heard most of the major works by Strauss and Debussy. I was surprised to find that the critics were still arguing about them. They first didn’t like them, then they praised them too much. In my opinion, Strauss was never better than Liszt.

In 1913, I heard Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps* in Paris. I wrote about it in my first book, published in 1915. It wasn’t until 1924, when the piece was finally played in New York, that the critics and conductors started to take Stravinsky seriously. That’s when they began to include his name on their programs. So, being a music critic in New York isn’t the best job for someone who has imagination and can see what’s coming.

There existed, beyond the mere inertia of professional allegiance, a more profound rationale for my withdrawal from the domain of musical critique—a rationale rooted in the dissonance between my temporal awareness and the myopic oscillations of those who purported to judge. I found myself perpetually ten years ahead of the critical establishment and the conductors who curated concert programs, a dissonant interval that rendered my perspective an anomaly in the symphonic discourse of the time. I had missed the vituperative discourse surrounding Wagner in New York, yet I had observed the press’s shifting valuations of Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, their initial disdain giving way, through repeated exposure, to begrudging acceptance—until these composers, once alien, were enshrined within the sacred canon. My orchestral tutelage under Theodore Thomas in Chicago, though not marked by the pantheon of conducting excellence, was grounded in a singular conviction: that new music must be heard. Thomas, though not a great conductor, possessed a fidelity to innovation that led him to perform, as soon as possible, every significant European composition upon its debut. By 1906, when I arrived in New York, I had already engaged with the major works of Strauss and Debussy, and I was struck by the critics’ continued oscillation between underestimation and hyperbole, their judgment still tethered to the past. In Paris, in 1913, I encountered Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps*, and in 1915, I extolled it in my first book. It was not until 1924, when the work was finally performed in New York, that the critics and conductors, long reluctant, began to acknowledge Stravinsky’s place. Thus, the role of a music critic in New York is not a vocation suited to those with vision or foresight.

There was a far more profound reason for my desertion from the camp of musical criticism—a reason that gnawed at the edges of my patience like a relentless, unrelenting beast. I was always ten years ahead of the pack, of the critics who scribbled their judgments and the conductors who curated their programs with the care of a man arranging a funeral. I missed the uproar over Wagner in New York, but I watched as the press turned its venom on Richard Strauss, Debussy, and Stravinsky, only to, in the end, through sheer repetition and the dull ache of familiarity, accept these composers as part of some sacred, unshakable hierarchy. My orchestral education was forged under Theodore Thomas in Chicago—a man not great, though always honest in his readings, who believed in the power of new music. He played every significant European work as soon as it was heard abroad. By the time I arrived in New York in 1906, I had already listened to and assessed nearly all of Strauss and Debussy’s works up to that point. I was stunned to find the critics still arguing about them, first underpraising, then overpraising, for Strauss, in my mind, has never been a whit superior to Liszt. In Paris, in 1913, I heard Stravinsky’s *Sacre du Printemps* and much more of his music. I wrote a panegyric about it in my first book, published in 1915. By 1924, *Sacre du Printemps* had finally reached New York, and the critics, at last, had accepted Stravinsky. So too had the conductors, who, until four years prior, had scarcely allowed his name to grace their programs. The job of a music critic in New York, then, is no place for a man with imagination or the foresight to see beyond the noise.

First, there was a Teachers' Institute at the county-seat; and there distinguished guests of the superintendent taught the teachers fractions and spelling and other mysteries,—white teachers in the morning, Negroes at night. A picnic now and then, and a supper, and the rough world was softened by laughter and song. I remember how— But I wander. There came a day when all the teachers left the Institute and began the hunt for schools. I learn from hearsay (for my mother was mortally afraid of fire-arms) that the hunting of ducks and bears and men is wonderfully interesting, but I am sure that the man who has never hunted a country school has something to learn of the pleasures of the chase. I see now the white, hot roads lazily rise and fall and wind before me under the burning July sun; I feel the deep weariness of heart and limb as ten, eight, six miles stretch relentlessly ahead; I feel my heart sink heavily as I hear again and again, "Got a teacher? Yes." So I walked on and on—horses were too expensive—until I had wandered beyond railways, beyond stage lines, to a land of "varmints" and rattlesnakes, where the coming of a stranger was an event, and men lived and died in the shadow of one blue hill.

White teachers taught in the morning, and Black teachers in the evening. Sometimes there were picnics and suppers, and the hard world felt a little softer with laughter and music. I remember how— but I'm getting off track. One day, all the teachers left the Institute and started looking for schools. I heard from others (my mother was too scared of guns) that hunting ducks, bears, and people is exciting, but I'm certain that anyone who hasn't hunted a country school misses out on something special. I can still see the white roads winding under the hot July sun, feel the tiredness in my heart and legs as miles stretch ahead. I could hear again and again, "Got a teacher? Yes." So I kept walking, no horses were cheap, until I reached a place where there were "varmints" and rattlesnakes, where a stranger was a big deal, and people lived and died under the shadow of one blue hill.

Now I perceive the white, hot roads, lazily undulating beneath the burning July sun; I feel the profound exhaustion of heart and limb as ten, eight, six miles stretch relentlessly ahead; I sense my spirit falter as I hear again and again, “Got a teacher? Yes.” Thus I walked on, unrelenting—horses too costly—until I had wandered beyond railways, beyond stage lines, into a realm of “varmints” and rattlesnakes, where the arrival of a stranger was an event, and men lived and died in the shadow of one blue hill.

First, there existed a Teachers’ Institute at the county-seat, where distinguished guests of the superintendent, in the manner of initiates of an esoteric order, instructed the teachers in the arcane disciplines of fractions and spelling—white educators in the morning, Negroes at night. Occasional picnics and suppers, punctuated by laughter and song, momentarily softened the rough edges of the world. I remember how—yet I wander. A day arrived when all the teachers abandoned the Institute and embarked upon the hunt for schools. Sprinkled over hill and dale lay cabins and farmhouses, shut out from the world by the forests and the rolling hills toward the east. There I found at last a little school. Josie told me of it; she was a thin, homely girl of twenty, with a dark-brown face and thick, hard hair. I had crossed the stream at Watertown, and rested under the great willows; then I had gone to the little cabin in the lot where Josie was resting on her way to town. The gaunt farmer made me welcome, and Josie, hearing my errand, told me anxiously that they wanted a school over the hill; that but once since the war had a teacher been there; that she herself longed to learn,—and thus she ran on, talking fast and loud, with much earnestness and energy.

Sprinkled like forgotten coins across the hills and valleys stood cabins and farmhouses, cloaked by forests and the undulating hills to the east. There, at last, I found a little school. Josie, a lean, plain girl of twenty, with a dark-brown face and thick, unyielding hair, spoke of it. I had crossed the stream at Watertown, rested beneath the great willows, and made my way to the humble cabin where Josie paused on her journey to town. The gaunt farmer welcomed me with a nod. Josie, hearing my purpose, spoke with urgency, her voice a storm of longing—she told of the school beyond the hill, how since the war, only once had a teacher set foot there, and how she herself ached to learn, her words tumbling forth, fierce and full of fire.

While we have been learning calculus and economics; the theories of versification and genetics; conversational French and Ibsen, it is helpful to be reminded that the home-folks have not been altogether standing still—that Frank Chumbley is developing social finesse and religious fervor in circulating the ice cream, that Jessie Siegler is cultivating a love for the beautiful through the embroidery club, and that McKinley Miller is taking an elementary course in home economics by correspondence and by an occasional private lesson from the girl at Odin.

There is no agency like the home paper for developing a broad human interest and for keeping us in touch with the friendships and the ideals of our youth.

While students are engaged in the study of calculus, economics, versification, genetics, conversational French, and Ibsen, it is beneficial to recall that individuals at home have also been actively involved in various pursuits. Frank Chumbley is refining social skills and religious devotion through ice cream distribution. Jessie Siegler is fostering an appreciation for beauty via embroidery. McKinley Miller is enrolling in a home economics course through correspondence and occasional private instruction from a local woman. The home paper serves as an effective medium for cultivating a wide range of human interests and maintaining awareness of youthful friendships and ideals.

My bands of silk and miniver Momently grew heavier; The black gauze was beggarly thin; The ermine muffled mouth and chin; I could not suck the moonlight in. Harlequin in lozenges Of love and hate, I walked in these Striped and ragged rigmaroles; Along the pavement my footsoles Trod warily on living coals. Shouldering the thoughts I loathed, In their corrupt disguises clothed, Morality I could not tear From my ribs, to leave them bare Ivory in silver air. There I walked, and there I raged; The spiritual savage caged Within my skeleton, raged afresh To feel, behind a carnal mesh, The clean bones crying in the flesh.

I could not suck the moonlight in.

footsoles treading warily on living coals.  
Shouldering thoughts I loathed,  
cloaked in corrupt disguises—  
morality, I could not tear from my ribs,  
leaving them bare, ivory in silver air.  
There I walked, there I raged;  
the spiritual savage, caged within my bones,  
raged anew, feeling clean bones cry  
beneath the carnal mesh.

For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love, Or chide my palsy, or my gout, My five gray hairs, or ruined fortune flout, With wealth your state, your mind with arts improve, Take you a course, get you a place, Observe his honor, or his grace, Or the king's real, or his stamped face Contemplate; what you will, approve, So you will let me love. Alas, alas, who's injured by my love? What merchant's ships have my sighs drowned? Who says my tears have overflowed his ground? When did my colds a forward spring remove? When did the heats which my veins fill Add one more to the plaguy bill? Soldiers find wars, and lawyers find out still Litigious men, which quarrels move, Though she and I do love. For God's sake, hold your tongue and let me love.  
Don't scold my shaking hands or aching joints,  
Or laugh at my gray hair or lost money.  
Use your money to live well,  
Your mind to learn things.  
Get a job, respect the king,  
Or his picture, or his face.  
Do what you like, but let me love.  
Alas, who suffers from my love?  
Have my sighs sunk any ships?  
Have my tears ruined any land?  
When did my colds make spring better?  
When did my hot blood add to a fever list?  
Soldiers find war, lawyers find lawsuits,  
Even though she and I love each other.  
Call us what you want, we're made this way by love.  
Call her one thing, me another.  
We're like candles, and we burn at our own cost.

For God’s sake, keep your mouth shut, let me love—  
Or scold my trembling hands, my aching bones,  
My silvered hair, my broken purse, my groans,  
Your mind with learning, your soul with art refine.  
Take aim, rise up, secure your station,  
Honor the king, his face, his grace, his name,  
Or judge the world as you will, just let me claim  
The right to love. Alas, who suffers from my flame?  
What ships have sunk beneath my endless sighs?  
Who’s ground been flooded by my endless tears?  
When did my chills chase spring from the skies?  
When did my fevered blood add to the plague?  
Soldiers chase war, lawyers chase their cases,  
Still quarrels bloom where love’s two hearts embrace.  
Call us what you will—love forged our fate,  
Two birds, two flames, two tapers, burning bright,  
Our own cost, our own end, we’ll face, and fight.

Shall I compare thee to a summers day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, And summers lease hath all too short a date; Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, And often is his gold complexion dimm'd; And every fair from fair sometime declines, By chance or natures changing course untrimm'd; But thy eternal summer shall not fade, Nor lose possession of that fair thou owst; Nor shall death brag thou wanderst in his shade, When in eternal lines to time thou growst: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Shall I liken thee to a summer’s day? Thou art more sweet, more mild, more wise—  
Rough winds do rattle May’s tender blooms, and summer’s lease is brief, too brief.  
At times the sun’s eye blazes fierce, and oft its golden face is veiled.  
All beauty fades, all fair things fall, by fate or nature’s shifting tide.  
But thy eternal spring shall never wither, nor lose the grace thou ownest.  
Death cannot claim thee in his dark domain, when in these lines thou art reborn.  
So long as breath or sight remains, these words shall live, and live for thee.

Stella is sick, and in that sick-bed lies Sweetness, that breathes and pants as oft as she; And grace, sick too, such fine conclusions tries That sickness brags itself best graced to be. Beauty is sick, but sick in so fair guise That in that paleness beautys white we see; And joy, which is inseparate from these eyes, Stella now learns (strange case!) to weep in thee. Love moves thy pain, and like a faithful page, As thy looks stir, runs up and down, to make All folks prest at thy will thy pain to assuage; Nature with care sweats for her darlings sake, Knowing worlds pass, ere she enough can find Of such heaven stuff, to clothe so heavenly mind.

Stella lies frail, a vessel wrecked by ill,  
where Sweetness gasps, a moth in fevered flight;  
Grace, too, lies prone, her logic lost in thrall,  
as sickness crowns itself with grace's light.  
Beauty, a rose, lies pale, yet still divine,  
its pallor blooming like a ghostly hue;  
Joy, that shadowed twin of Stella’s eyes,  
now weeps, a stranger, in her soul’s new view.  
Love, a squire, runs wild through halls of ache,  
to soothe each soul with whispers of thy pain;  
Nature, in her haste, pours forth her grace,  
to clothe this mind, this heaven, with her rain.

Stella lies ailing, and within that chamber of affliction, Sweetness breathes and labors as if in concert with her; Grace, too, succumbs, attempting in its frailty to articulate the grandeur of sickness, which, in its own perverse way, claims to be the most adorned. Beauty, though afflicted, presents itself in such refined guise that even in pallor, its whiteness becomes a revelation. Joy, ever entwined with these eyes, now, in this strange circumstance, learns to weep for Stella. Love, like a devoted scribe, moves in response to her gaze, traversing the world to ease her suffering. Nature, in its tender care, toils ceaselessly for her beloved, knowing that countless worlds may pass before it can gather enough of celestial essence to clothe such a divine mind.

Home I return, in song’s embrace, one with thee, no more to fly.  
My song, my soul, my life, my all—what need of prayer or plea?  
For I am already one with thee, in melody, in thee, in me.

Perspective never withers from their eyes; They keep that docile edict of the Spring That blends March with August Antarctic skies: These are but cows that see no other thing Than grass and snow, and their own inner being Through the rich halo that they do not trouble Even to cast upon the seasons fleeting Though they should thin and die on last years stubble. Perspective never withers in their gaze—  
They hold that gentle law of Spring,  
That fuses March with August’s frozen blue,  
As if the world were but a herd of cows  
Who see no more than grass and snow,  
Their own inner light refracted through  
A halo they never lift to cast  
On seasons that flicker and fade,  
Leaving stubble where last year’s frost  
Still clings to the earth. They are clumsy,  
Hefty, unflinching—while we,  
Pressing the cider mill, watch them  
With eyes that taste the bitter sweetness  
Of friendships turned to vinegar,  
Of phlegm that lingers, of reprisals  
That shift like shadows, till we wonder  
When the jest becomes too sharp to be kind.  
We boast of faith in others,  
Who would, themselves, chase the merriest ghost.  
Above them, old Mizzentop,  
White palace, floor by floor,  
Stacks its stoic height in dormer windows,  
Staring out toward what once was.

Care for thy soul as thing of greatest price, Made to the end to taste of power divine, Devoid of guilt, abhorring sin and vice, Apt by Gods grace to virtue to incline. Care for it so as by thy retchless train It be not brought to taste eternal pain. Care for thy corse, but chiefly for souls sake; Cut off excess, sustaining food is best; To vanquish pride but comely clothing take; Seek after skill, deep ignorance detest. Care so, I say, the flesh to feed and clothe That thou harm not thy soul and body both. Care for the world to do thy body right; Rack not thy wit to win thy wicked ways; Seek not to oppress the weak by wrongful might; To pay thy due do banish all delays. Care to dispend according to thy store, And in like sort be mindful of the poor. Care for thy soul, as for thy chiefest stay; Care for thy body for thy souls avail; Care for the world for bodys help alway; Care yet but so as virtue may prevail. Care in such sort that thou be sure of this: Care keep thee not from heaven and heavenly bliss.

Care for thy soul, that sovereign entity, as the sole currency of divine potency, unshackled from the chains of guilt and the corruption of vice, its trajectory steered by celestial grace toward the ascendance of virtue. Let not thy relentless indulgence corrupt it, lest it be consigned to the abyss of eternal anguish. Attend to thy flesh, yet prioritize the soul’s preservation; curtail excess, for sustenance is the minimal requisite. Reject pride, yet accept modest adornment; pursue mastery, abhor ignorance. Nourish and clothe thy body, yet ensure neither soul nor form is compromised. Engage the world to serve thy corporeal needs, but let not thy intellect be enslaved to base desires; resist the temptation to dominate the weak through unjust force. Fulfill thy obligations, and let no delay impede thy duty. Distribute thy resources with prudence, and extend thy care to the destitute. Let thy soul be thy steadfast anchor; let thy body serve its purpose; let the world be a tool for thy existence, yet always subordinate to the triumph of virtue. In this manner, ensure that thy care does not sever thee from the divine and the bliss of the heavens.

Care for thy soul, that sacred, priceless thing,  
A vessel meant to drink of divine might,  
Free from the weight of guilt, sin’s cruel sting,  
Guided by grace to virtue’s holy light.  
Let not thy reckless ways lead it to pain,  
A fate etched deep in hell’s unyielding chain.  
Tend to thy flesh, but let the soul be first—  
Cut off the excess, let food be thy nurse.  
Pride must be slain, yet dress with modest grace;  
Seek wisdom’s fire, shun the dark embrace.  
Nourish thy flesh, yet harm not soul or frame,  
For both are bound in one, a sacred name.  
Care for the world to serve thy body’s need,  
Let not thy wit be shackled to deceit.  
Oppress not the weak with might unjustly spread;  
Pay thy due, and let no delay be said.  
Spend with care, and tend to those in need,  
For virtue’s flame must never be unseed.  
In all thou dost, let care be thy command—  
That heaven’s door may not be barred by hand.

Blame thy self, and nott my folly, Time gave time butt to bee holly; True love such ends best loveth Unworhty love doth seeke for ends A worthy love butt worth pretends Nor other thoughts itt proveth: Then stay thy swiftnes cruell time, And lett mee once more blessed clime To joy, that I may prayse thee: Lett mee pleasure sweetly tasting Joy in love, and faith nott wasting And on fames wings Ile rayse thee: Never shall thy glory dying Bee untill thine owne untying That time noe longer liveth; Tis a gaine such tyme to lend: Since soe thy fame shall never end Butt joy for what she giveth.

Time, thou thief of my unrest,  
By whom I once hoped to be blest—  
How cruel art thou, turned?  
That first gave life unto my love,  
And still a pleasure not to move  
Or change, though ever burned.  
Have I thee slack'd, or left undone  
One loving rite, and so have won  
Thy rage or bitter changing?  
That now no minutes I shall see,  
Wherein I may least happy be—  
Thy favors so estranging.  

Blame thy self, and not my folly,  
Time gave time, but to be holly;  
True love such ends best loveth,  
Unworthy love doth seek for ends,  
A worthy love but worth pretends,  
Nor other thoughts it proveth.  

Then stay thy swiftness, cruel time,  
And let me once more blessed climb  
To joy, that I may praise thee:  
Let me pleasure sweetly tasting,  
Joy in love, and faith not wasting,  
And on fame’s wings I’ll raise thee.  

Never shall thy glory dying  
Be until thine own untying—  
That time no longer liveth;  
’Tis a gain such time to lend:  
Since so thy fame shall never end,  
But joy for what she giveth.

Time is the cause of my trouble,  
By whom I once hoped to be blessed.  
How cruel you are, you who first gave life  
To my love, and still bring joy without  
Change or movement, though you burn.  
Have I neglected any loving act,  
And so won your anger or bitter change?  
Now I see no minutes where I may be  
Least unhappy, as your favor turns away.  
Blame yourself, not my foolishness.  
Time gave time, but only to be holly.  
True love best loves without end,  
Unworthy love seeks ends,  
A worthy love only worth pretends,  
And no other thoughts it proves.  
So stay your swift pace, cruel time,  
Let me once more reach the blessed joy  
To praise you. Let me taste sweet pleasure,  
Joy in love, and faith not lost.  
On fame’s wings I’ll raise you:  
Never shall your glory die  
Until your own untieing.  
Time no longer lives;  
It’s a gain such time to lend.  
Since then your fame shall never end,  
But joy for what she gives.

Blame thy self, and not my folly; time gave time but to be holly; true love such ends best loveth, unworthy love doth seek for ends, a worthy love but worth pretends, nor other thoughts it proveth: then stay thy swiftness, cruel time, and let me once more blessed clime to joy, that I may praise thee: let me pleasure sweetly tasting, joy in love, and faith not wasting, and on fames wings I'll raise thee: never shall thy glory dying be until thine own untying, that time no longer liveth; tis a gain such tyme to lend: since so thy fame shall never end, but joy for what she giveth.

Sweet shades why doe you seeke to give delight To mee who deeme delight in this vilde place Butt torment, sorrow, and mine owne disgrace To taste of joy, or your vaine pleasing sight; Show them your pleasures who saw never night Of greife, wher joyings fauning, smiling face Appeers as day, wher griefe found never space Yett for a sigh, a grone, or envies spite; Butt O on mee a world of woes doe ly, Or els on mee all harmes strive to rely, And to attend like servants bound to mee, Heat in desire, while frosts of care I prove, Wanting my love, yett surfett doe with love Burne, and yett freeze, better in hell to bee.

Sweet shades, why seek to gift me joy, I who find delight in this bleak, wild place—yet torment, sorrow, and my own disgrace are what I crave, to taste of your hollow, fleeting sight. Show them your pleasures, those who’ve never known night of grief, where joy’s fleeting smile appears as day, where sorrow never found a place. Yet for a sigh, a groan, or envy’s spite—O, let a world of woes lie on me, or let all harms rely on me, servants bound to my despair. Heat in desire, while frosts of care I prove, wanting your love, yet drowned in it. Burn, and yet freeze—better in hell to be.

Whoso list to hunt, I know where is an hind, But as for me, helas, I may no more. The vain travail hath wearied me so sore, I am of them that farthest cometh behind. Yet may I by no means my wearied mind Draw from the deer, but as she fleeth afore Fainting I follow. I leave off therefore, Sithens in a net I seek to hold the wind. Who list her hunt, I put him out of doubt, As well as I may spend his time in vain. And graven with diamonds in letters plain There is written, her fair neck round about: Noli me tangere, for Caesar's I am, And wild for to hold, though I seem tame.

Whosoever seeks the chase, I discern the stag's whereabouts; yet, alas, I am bereft of further pursuit. The futility of endeavor has drained me, rendering me the last among the hunters. Still, my weary mind cannot cease its chase, though she flees ahead, and I, fainting, follow in her wake. Hence, I desist, for in a snare I attempt to grasp the wind. To those who would pursue her, I offer this: my efforts are but a waste of time. Inscribed upon her graceful neck, in diamond script, it reads: "Noli me tangere," for she is Caesar's, wild to be held, though she appears tame.

Caesar’s own, wild as the storm’s first cry,  
And tame, though I may seem, I still pursue.

My true-love hath my heart and I have his, By just exchange one for the other given: I hold his dear, and mine he cannot miss; There never was a bargain better driven. His heart in me keeps me and him in one; My heart in him his thoughts and senses guides: He loves my heart, for once it was his own; I cherish his because in me it bides. His heart his wound received from my sight; My heart was wounded with his wounded heart; For as from me on him his hurt did light, So still, methought, in me his hurt did smart: Both equal hurt, in this change sought our bliss, My true love hath my heart and I have his.

Farewell friend wantcatcher, since 'twill not be, Thou cannot catch the wants, but they catch me.

Now in the West the slender moon lies low, And now Orion glimmers through the trees, Clearing the earth with even pace and slow, And now the stately-moving Pleiades, In that soft infinite darkness overhead Hang jewel-wise upon a silver thread. And all the lonelier stars that have their place, Calm lamps within the distant southern sky, And planet-dust upon the edge of space, Look down upon the fretful world, and I Look up to outer vastness unafraid And see the stars which sang when earth was made.

Now in the West the slender moon dips low,  
And Orion flickers through the whispering trees,  
Clearing the earth with even, slow grace,  
While the Pleiades, stately and wise,  
Hang jewel-wise on a silver thread in the dark.  
The lonelier stars, calm lamps in the south,  
And planet-dust at the edge of space,  
Look down on the fretful world, and I  
Rise to the vast, unafraid,  
And see the stars that sang when earth was made.

The Pleiades, those stately constellations, hang suspended in the infinite dark, jewels strung upon a silvery thread. Potuia, potuia White grave goddess, Pity my sadness, O silence of Paros. I am not of these about thy feet, These garments and decorum; I am thy brother, Thy lover of aforetime crying to thee, And thou hearest me not. I have whispered thee in thy solitudes Of our loves in Phrygia, The far ecstasy of burning noons When the fragile pipes Ceased in the cypress shade, And the brown fingers of the shepherd Moved over slim shoulders; And only the cicada sang. I have told thee of the hills And the lisp of reeds And the sun upon thy breasts, And thou hearest me not, Potuia, potuia Thou hearest me not.

I have whispered thee in thy solitudes of our loves in Phrygia, the far ecstasy of burning noons when the fragile pipes ceased in the cypress shade, and the brown fingers of the shepherd moved over slim shoulders; and only the cicada sang. I have told thee of the hills, the lisp of reeds, and the sun upon thy breasts, and thou hearest me not, Potuia, Potuia—thou hearest me not.
